title: Texans' Secondary Expected to See One Key Change vs. Colts
full_text:
This season, the Houston Texans' secondary has not been the elite unit it once was back during their 2025 campaign.
Through the first nine games of the season, the Texans have found themselves ranked 27th in the NFL for opposing passing yards allowed (2,165), have hauled in just five interceptions, and sit right in the middle of the pack for net passing yards allowed per attempt (6.2).
With that lowly production in mind, DeMeco Ryans and the Texans' staff decided to make a small shift within their secondary before facing off against the Cleveland Browns this past weekend.
Rather than starting Reed Blankenship as their strong safety next to Calen Bullock in the back-end, they rolled out veteran M.J. Stewart as their second starting safety–– despite Blankenship being deemed healthy from his concussion/hand injury after missing the prior two games because of it.
And that setup in the secondary didn't quite pan out as well as the Texans might've expected .
Houston saw Deshaun Watson to throw for over 300 yards, Stewart allowed a season-high 86 yards, along with three receptions for the seven plays he was targeted on, and course, the Texans came up short against Cleveland in a humbling 24-27 loss.
So heading into the Texans' Thursday Night Football matchup against the Indianapolis Colts less than one week later, it seems as if Houston will be making another pivot within their secondary in hopes that it can result in a better output.
According to a recent report from James Palmer of NFL on Prime , the Texans will be set to start Blankenship once again in their safety unit next to Bullock against the Colts.
A couple of updates regarding the secondaries for tonight. For the #colts Sauce Gardner (left calf ... again) won't play tonight I'm told. And for the #texans Reed Blankenship will be back in at safety next to Calen Bullock.
That means for Stewart, he'll be due to revert back to his role as a backup within the Texans' safety unit. Houston will be hoping that their previous tandem in the back-end of Bullock and Blankenship will be more successful than what was seen this past weekend, and really, for most of this season.
Blankenship, who the Texans signed to a three-year, $24 million deal this past offseason , hasn't quite paid off as the investment Houston thought they were initially getting.
Blakenship was expected to enter the Texans' safety unit as a stabilizing force next to Bullock, with impressive leadership qualities, Super Bowl pedigree, and a physical nature that fits well alongside the rest of Houston's "SWARM" mindset on that side of the ball.
Instead, Blankenship has had quite the opposite effect.
He's shown clear signs of regression compared to his time with the Philadelphia Eagles, has struggled to adjust to Houston's scheme, is allowing the highest opposing passer rating of his career when targeted (112.9), and is currently on pace to destroy his highest yards allowed in a season.
It also didn't help Blankenship's case when he went down with a concussion in Week 6 against the Jacksonville Jaguars , and was ultimately sidelined a little longer than expected as he was recovering from hand surgery.
Seeing that he was limited to just two snaps when healthy against the Browns, the writing felt as if it were on the wall that Blankenship had been unofficially benched, and the defense was simply going to roll with the combination of Stewart and Bullock in the back-end until further notice.
Yet, just one game later, Blankenship has reportedly gotten the call-up once again for a chance of redemption within the Texans' defense.
Time will tell if the decision will pay off for the Texans and their defensive success. But in a matchup against the Colts and quarterback Daniel Jones ––who currently leads the league in total interceptions (12)––the stage could be set for a get-right game to be in the works for not just Blankenship individually, but for Houston's secondary as a whole.

title: Why Texans' Will Anderson Is Set Up for a Monster Night vs. Colts
full_text:
The Houston Texans have a must-win matchup on tap against the Indianapolis Colts for Thursday Night Football .
Houston's back is against the wall with a 3-6 record. They’re coming off a brutal loss this past weekend against the Cleveland Browns. Another loss to the 3-7 Indianapolis Colts might just be a death sentence for any hope at a similar rise up the standings in the second half of the season like they saw in 2025.
So the pressure is on for this Texans team to bring the heat on Thursday night. And when taking a step back to see what both sides will be working with in this game, there's be good reason to feel optimistic about Houston's chances to come away with a win on their home field on a short week.
And really, a lot of those positive feelings for the Texans' chances might be because of what we could expect from Will Anderson , who could have a serious opportunity to put together one of his best individual performances of the season so far.
Of course, any time that Anderson takes the field for the Texans, he's prone to have a dominant individual performance. There's a reason he currently leads the league in total sacks after 10 weeks of the season.
But there's a clear route for Anderson to really have a night to remember against the Colts, which not only comes because of the situation on the Texans' defensive line, yet also due to what Indianapolis’s offensive line is shaping up to look like on Thursday night.
For one, the Texans will be without Danielle Hunter for a second straight game with a hamstring injury.
With that in mind, Jadeveon Clowney is due to claim Hunter's starting reps and likely be on the field for a little over 75% of the defensive snaps, while Anderson will continue in his usual role as the head of the snake for Houston's pass rush.
Last weekend against the Browns, Anderson was in the same situation. Without Hunter, he finished the game with four total tackles, a sack, and a forced fumble. A pretty solid game for his standards. But against the Colts, there could be room for even more out of the Texans' All-Pro.
That's due to the absences that the Colts will be dealing with on their offensive front . Both of their starting tackles, Bernhard Raimann and Jalen Travis, will be sidelined due to injury, and thus potentially places Charlie Heck and Matt Goncalves in line to start on the left and right side of Indianapolis's line, respectively.
Heck has yet to see a single offensive snap for the Colts this season. Goncalves, while a respectable right guard, has only moved outside to right tackle for 59 total snaps this season.
That sets up a golden opportunity for Anderson––and really, the rest of the Texans' pass rush––to take advantage of a major mismatch, even if they are without Hunter as a part of the equation.
The last time the Texans faced off against the Colts in Week 3 , we saw Houston's defensive line combine for four total sacks, while Anderson saw 2.5 go his way. This time, it wouldn't be shocking to see Anderson have a repeat performance of such a stat line, or simply have a better night altogether.
And if that does happen to come to fruition, it becomes pretty hard to imagine Houston not being able to split their season series against the Colts in a must-win primetime matchup.

title: 3 Bold Texans Predictions for How TNF Matchup vs. Colts Could Go
full_text:
The Houston Texans have their first primetime game of the 2026 season on tap for Thursday night, as they'll be tasked with their second matchup of the year against their AFC rival, the Indianapolis Colts.
Based on how the odds are looking heading into this contest , many are expecting the night to be a bit one-sided in the hands of the Texans on their home field on a short week.
But as with any divisional matchup in the NFL, there's always bound to be some unexpected surprises to unfold that make the events pan out a bit differently than the general consensus expects.
With that in mind, let's sort through a batch of three bold predictions on how Thursday night's action could look between the Texans and Colts:
The Texans have seen firsthand just how ugly things can get for the Colts and their offense when Daniel Jones is feeling turnover-happy. In their Week 3 matchup, it was Jones who gave up three turnovers between two interceptions and a fumble, and still managed to claw out a narrow 19-17 victory .
It's hard to imagine the Texans winning the turnover battle 3-0 and still coming up short once again. On the other hand, it might not be too tough to picture Jones struggling with his ball security in another matchup against this defense, especially when factoring in a short week on the road without many reliable weapons in his arsenal of pass-catchers.
On the season, Jones is averaging nearly two turnovers a game between his league-leading 12 interceptions and five fumbles. If the Texans take an early lead, and the game script forces the Colts to keep throwing the ball, the door could be wide open for Houston to capitalize on multiple errors from Indianapolis' signal-caller.
The stage feels like it's set for a monster game to come from Texans' All-Pro edge rusher Will Anderson Jr.
For one, the Texans are forced to enter this matchup without Danielle Hunter for the second straight game due to a hamstring injury. That means Houston will have to rely on Anderson to carry a bit more of the load within the pass-rush than usual–– but considering he leads the lead in total sacks through 10 weeks, we know he's more than capable of doing just that.
On top of Hunter's absence, though, the Colts will be dealing with some key injuries on their offensive line to starting tackles Bernhard Raimann and Jalen Travis.
So Anderson––one of the best pass-rushers the NFL has to offer––will have the opportunity to go up against a pair of backup tackles on the Colts line coming off a short week. Anderson has already had one game this season logging three sacks against the Tennessee Titans in Week 5, and maybe Indianapolis is the next AFC South opponent up to face that same fate on Thursday.
The Texans have had multiple games this season in which they've struggled immensely in keeping their penalties down. In fact, four of their last six games have resulted in Houston getting called for 10 or more penalties.
Last weekend against the Cleveland Browns, things got as bad as we've seen this season , as the Texans were called for a season-high 13 penalties and 112 yards. Impressively enough, four of those penalties were caused because of their special teams unit.
Could the Texans magically turn a corner in this game and look like a more disciplined, refined unit to limit the penalties? It's always possible. Maybe the solution to those penalty problems finally clicked for DeMeco Ryans and this coaching staff after the events of last weekend.
But we're now over halfway into the regular season, and Houston is still dealing with those excessive flags, just as they did over the course of 2025. So it's easy to see how this team could have yet another week of 10 or more penalties, especially on a short week of preparation.

title: Colts Position Grades: Another Embarrassing Divisional Beatdown
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts were embarrassed under the bright lights Thursday night, falling 26-3 to the Houston Texans in a game that somehow looked even worse than the scoreboard suggests.
Indianapolis (3-8) managed just eight first downs, 167 total yards, and went 1-for-11 on third down. Houston scored 26 unanswered after the Colts' opening field goal.
Everything about this team looks uninspired. And somehow, the defense is now giving us more hope than the offense, something you never would've guessed watching the first few weeks of this season.
It's the Colts' second straight road divisional beatdown. Here are my Week 11 position grades.
Daniel Jones has to go. I still think he's this team's best quarterback, and I don't dislike him, but 12-of-27 for 144 yards and an interception simply isn't getting it done.
To his credit, he pushed the ball downfield more than usual before Anthony Richardson entered late. At this point, Shane Steichen has to seriously consider making a change at quarterback, even if no one on this roster would look good behind this line.
Jonathan Taylor and Seth McGowan combined for just 28 rushing yards, with McGowan exiting due to a hamstring injury.
When the passing attack is this hopeless, you have to have success running the ball. This was a piss-poor performance.
Anthony Gould led the group with 48 receiving yards, and no other wideout topped 30.
Poor quarterback play doesn't help, but these guys aren't consistently creating separation, either.
Tyler Warren's lone catch for 22 yards accounted for the entire position group's receiving production.
Add in the horrible blocking, and there's not much positive to say here.
Both starting tackles were out, and boy, did it show.
Houston's front absolutely feasted all night, generating pressure on more than half of Indianapolis' dropbacks while the rushing attack managed just 38 yards.
Adetomiwa Adebawore remains the lone bright spot, recording seven pressures, seven tackles, and the Colts' only sack.
Adebawore entered Week 9 leading NFL defensive tackles with a 16.1% pressure rate, but the rest of this group got bullied, particularly against the run.
CJ Allen continues to look like a legitimate building block, finishing with a game-high 16 tackles.
Bryce Boettcher had his moments, but beyond Allen, this was a pretty average night.
Missing Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward certainly hurt, but the remaining corners were dismantled.
C.J. Stroud finished 21-of-27 with three touchdowns, and Houston found big plays whenever it needed them.
A.J. Haulcy grabbed his first career interception, while Cam Bynum nearly had another before replay overturned it.
The safeties weren't perfect, but they were probably the defense's best unit.
Spencer Shrader finished 1-for-3, missing from 56 yards before having a 62-yarder blocked.
Difficult kicks, sure, but execution from this unit was downright bad.
At 3-8, this team isn't just losing. It's getting embarrassed, and unless something changes quickly, things could get even uglier in Indianapolis.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly From Another Frustrating Colts’ Performance
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts had another difficult night against the Houston Texans, losing 26-3 in frustrating fashion yet again. Additionally, the performance left plenty of questions about where this team goes from here.
With the season continuing to slip away, the margin for error is getting smaller and the pressure is mounting on an organization that needs to find some answers. As always, there were a few positives to take away, but the overall performance offered another reminder of just how much work remains ahead.
Let's take a look at the good, the bad and the ugly from Indianapolis' faceplant in primetime.
Seth McGowan was one of the few Colts players who provided a genuine spark before his afternoon was cut short by a hamstring injury.
The rookie running back gave Indianapolis some much-needed explosiveness in the return game, ripping off kickoff returns of 30, 40 and 47 yards to give the offense solid starting field position. His role as a rusher before leaving the game was limited to just three carries for seven yards, but the Colts continue to show belief in their young rusher.
Unfortunately, McGowan's injury overshadowed what had been a promising showing. His ability to create big plays in the return game gives Indianapolis another potential avenue for generating offense and could make him a valuable contributor as he continues to develop.
The Colts have spent much of the season searching for reliable production beyond their established playmakers, and McGowan was showing signs of being able to provide some of that. Losing him, even temporarily, would be an unfortunate setback for a young player who was beginning to find his footing in the NFL
Adetomiwa Adebawore continues to be one of the more encouraging developments on the Colts' defensive line. While the unit as a whole struggled to generate pressure and make life difficult for C.J. Stroud, Adebawore was once again the exception, logging the only sack of the evening, despite facing frequent double teams.
Tomi time. 💥 📺Prime pic.twitter.com/PNQEQjK2zn
Adebawore has increasingly become the player Indianapolis can rely on to create disruption up front, and that distinction is particularly important given how little production the Colts have received from the rest of their defensive front.
His continued emergence is especially encouraging after his contract extension. The organization clearly believes there is another level to Adebawore's game, and his recent performances are beginning to provide some evidence that the investment could pay off.
However, an extension also raises expectations. There is still development ahead, but having a young defensive lineman begin to establish himself as a legitimate building block is an important positive for a unit with plenty of questions to answer.
Indianapolis just needs more players to follow Adebawore's lead.
If there is one thing the Colts can take away from Thursday night, it's that their defensive rookies continue to show encouraging signs despite the team's overall struggles. CJ Allen, Bryce Boettcher and AJ Haulcy each had moments worth recognizing, and I wanted to give them each their flowers.
Allen continues to demonstrate an impressive combination of speed, instincts and intelligence. His ability to find the football and consistently make tackles has become a defining part of his early contributions. With a team-leading 15-tackle game, that's now three double-digit tackle performances in the last four for Allen.
Boettcher has similarly shown an ability to be around the football and contribute in the middle of the defense, finding his way into the backfield and even making a play to force a turnover on downs late in the game.
Haulcy's rookie season has been rocky, but snagging his first NFL interception should be a nice confidence boost.
AJ HAULCY!!! 📺 Prime pic.twitter.com/tbGSSROK37
None of these players are finished products, and there will undoubtedly be growing pains down the road. But Allen, Boettcher and Haulcy are showing that Indianapolis may have found some legitimate young talent through the draft that they can build around. That on its own is worth some optimism.
The Colts' defensive line once again demonstrated just how much work remains to be done before this unit can be considered a reliable strength of the defense.
Indianapolis struggled to generate meaningful pressure on C.J. Stroud throughout the first half, failing to get any pressure on the pocket and allowing the Texans quarterback to sit comfortably in the pocket and survey the field. Outside of Adebawore, there was very little disruption, leaving Houston with far too much freedom to operate.
But the problem goes beyond the lack of sacks. A pass rush that can't consistently influence the passer is a pass rush that doesn't work. The Colts were largely unable to do that. When Stroud had the time to work through his progressions and wait for receivers to uncover against a depleted secondary, it's game over.
The bigger concern is what this performance says about the personnel Indianapolis currently has available. Adebawore's emergence is encouraging, but one player cannot be expected to carry an entire defensive front. The Colts need more consistent contributions from their defensive tackles and edge rushers, particularly if they want to compete against the better quarterbacks in the AFC.
If the unit cannot generate pressure without blitzing or relying on individual efforts, it will remain a unit that's made no progress from a year ago, and arguably has gotten worse.
Shane Steichen continues to make decisions that raise legitimate questions about his ability to get the most out of this football team.
Indianapolis had no offense to speak of, yet there has been little indication that Steichen has found a reliable solution. Daniel Jones---who Steichen continues to stand by for seemingly no reason---and the rest of the players have not been put in particularly favorable positions to succeed. He even forced Spencer Shrader to try two field goals from 56 and 62 yards respectively in the first half, one which he missed and one which was blocked, giving Houston great field position against a banged up defense. A prime example of setting your players up for failure.
When the offense is as inept at this, it's a reflection of one person, and one person only.
The larger issue is that Steichen appears to be running out of answers. His continued commitment to Jones is reaching impossible-to-defend status, and there needs to be some accountability for the lack of progress.
Steichen needs to demonstrate that he can still lead the Colts in the right direction. Right now, there is very little evidence that he can.
The sophomore slump continues for Tyler Warren, who managed just one catch for 22 yards.
Warren has been one of the more promising pieces of the Colts' offense this season, making his quiet night another frustrating development in a passing game that desperately needs reliable contributors. His first two targets were both difficult opportunities, with one getting tipped and another arriving at his feet. When Warren finally managed to make a reception, it came on a dangerous throw that left him shaken up.
It would be unfair to place much of the blame for his limited production on Warren himself. The opportunities simply have not been there, and the lack of any threat at wide receiver makes it easier for defenses to key in on him against the pass.
Warren is an important part of the team's long-term plans, and his ability to contribute as both a receiver and blocker makes him a valuable weapon. But Thursday night was just further proof that Warren can't be a one-man band.
The Colts need to do a better job of utilizing Warren. Whether that means creating more opportunities underneath, moving him around the formation or incorporating him more deliberately into the progression, he should be a consistent part of the offensive game plan.

title: Biggest Takeaway From Colts' Loss to Texans: Shane Steichen Might Finally Bench Daniel Jones
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts fall to 3-8 on the year after getting handled with ease by the Houston Texans on primetime television by a score of 26-3.
This soon-to-be forgotten Thursday Night Football showdown has split the divisional series for the year and has given the Texans a much-needed bump in playoff probability.
But what has changed for the Indianapolis Colts' outlook?
As far as this season is concerned, almost nothing at all.
We're leaving Week 11 almost the same way we entered it, though there could be reason to believe that some change(s) could be made following the loss in question.
This all leads to one question, one that I try to answer below.
At this point, Shane Steichen's steadfast belief in Daniel Jones is not just unwarranted, it's unacceptable.
The longest leash in recent memory has stretched out for too long , and now the Colts are losing valuable reps.
It wouldn't be surprising if the Colts lost every remaining game on their schedule, so one might think a personnel change wouldn't change things, but it's more than that.
Of course, there's a reality where the Colts' offense manages to play worse that they have for the vast majority of this season if they were to turn to either Anthony Richardson or Riley Leonard, but there's no harm is trying.
Again, the Colts' season is lost, and although a quarterback change is unlikely to change their bleak outlook, the offensive players who are contractually set to enter the rebuild could benefit from a new face leading the charge .
But even then, surely either Richardson or Leonard could do better than what Daniel Jones has shown as of late . Jones has struggled all season long, but he's especially done so in recent weeks.
Most recently, against the Houston Texans on Thursday Night Football, Daniel Jones went 12-27 (44.4% completion) for 144 passing yards, one interception, and was sacked twice.
Tonight's loss supported the notion that Daniel Jones is the least successful quarterback in primetime history , given that he now sports the worst record of all-time at 1-17. Quarterback wins are a flawed statistic in general, but there's some truth to Jones not showing up when the lights are brightest.
Speaking to his aforementioned bad stretch leading up to tonight, here's how Daniel Jones had fared in the Colts' previous four games:
1. 13-22 (59.1%) 108 pass yards, 1 INT 2. 19-28 (67.9%) 144 pass yards, 1 TD, 2 INTs 3. 20-34 (58.8%) 180 pass yards, 1 TD, 1 INT 4. 11-22 (50%) 108 pass yards, 1 TD, 2 INTs
Jones remains the league-leader in interceptions thrown after having thrown his thirteenth against the Texans, and now we'll have to see if Shane Steichen finally makes a permanent switch.
Anthony Richardson did relieve Jones of his duties late in the fourth quarter once the game was already decided. This is the second time Steichen has benched Jones late in a lost game this season, and given that Jones remained the starting quarterback after the fact, it's fair to assume that he'll continue trotting him out for the foreseeable future.
History suggests that Steichen will ride with Jones until the wheels fall off, but he should've put a pin in this experience weeks ago, and now there's simply no reason not to turn to somebody else.
After all, Steichen's job is on the line, so one would think the sense of urgency, the same one that Colts' principal owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon talked about going into the season, would convince him to do whatever's necessary to right the ship, but alas.
For weeks, Steichen has pointed out that the situation around Jones is untenable, but he's also continued to say that he has to take care of the ball moving forward.
Steichen has also said that he's been evaluating the need for a quarterback change for several weeks, but despite ample evidence to suggest a move is not just warranted but also necessary, he's stood pat.
#Colts HC Shane Steichen on how he decides if a QB change is needed: “I always go back and look at the film and make sure, on this play, was it his fault or someone else's fault? Obviously, the biggest thing is taking care of the football moving forward.” pic.twitter.com/kugbpBtERW
Well, with each passing week, Jones has failed to do just that.
Daniel Jones has now thrown an interception in 10 of his 11 games played after Thursday Night Football, and has thrown an interception in six straight games.
It'd be one thing if Jones was a gunslinger who was scoring more touchdowns than he was turning the ball over, but it's been the opposite. Jones has accounted for double the amount of turnovers (16 - interceptions, 3 fumbles lost) as he has touchdowns scored (8 - 7 passing, 1 rushing).
Whatever the case may be, whether the unsustainable offensive product is solely on the quarterback play, if it's a trickle-down effect from the offense's league-worst supporting cast, or both, one thing is undeniable: whatever level of preparation that Daniel Jones puts in to earn his keep is not enough.
Now, with the Colts entering a longer week of practice after being dealt a short week, turning to Richardson or Leonard seems more likely than before. Performance was the main reason that the benching talks became so strong in the first place, but now logistics and future development are coming together to improve the argument altogether.
The Indianapolis Colts should have benched Daniel Jones weeks ago , but at least there's now enough reason to believe Shane Steichen might actually do it.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Colts vs. Texans Best Bets: 3 Props to Target on Thursday Night
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts haven't given bettors much reason for optimism, and Thursday night's primetime matchup with the Houston Texans isn't changing that.
At 3-7, Indianapolis is playing some downright ugly football. Houston is only 3-6, but the Texans enter as massive favorites for good reason.
Still, this is an AFC South rivalry under the lights. The Colts already beat Houston 19-17 earlier this season, and in divisional games, anything can happen.
When a team looks this bad, there's often value hiding in the rubble. We're 17-10 on Colts-specific best bets this season, and I'm looking to keep that momentum going.
Here are my three best bets for Thursday night.
At plus money, I absolutely love the value here.
Look, I get it. This Colts offense can barely move the football, and facing Houston's defensive front won't make life any easier for Daniel Jones.
But I think Indianapolis can cross midfield a few times. Actually punching the ball into the end zone? That's a different story.
That should give Spencer Shrader plenty of opportunities, and he's been one of the few reliable players on this roster.
Shrader is 23-for-25 on field goals, with his only misses coming against Minnesota. He's cleared this line six times, including a perfect 4-for-4 performance against Houston in Week 3.
Even better, he's made nine of his 10 attempts from 50-plus yards and is tied for the NFL lead with 88 kicking points.
If the Colts get anywhere near scoring range, I trust Shrader to cash this ticket.
Daniel Jones doesn't have many proven weapons left, which makes Ashton Dulin an interesting target at such a low number.

He's not a high-volume receiver, and we’re not pretending he'll suddenly become one. But with this passing attack desperate for a spark, I expect Shane Steichen to find creative ways to get him involved.
One catch could be all we need.
The Colts defense has looked better lately, but let's not get carried away. Their last two opponents, Miami and Dallas, are a combined 5-14.
Now Indianapolis faces a Houston team favored by double digits, and I expect the Texans to lean on their ground game.
David Montgomery scored three touchdowns in Week 1 but hasn't found the end zone since. After missing four games with a groin injury, he's set to return with Woody Marks ruled out.
That should give Montgomery plenty of opportunities near the goal line.
I'm betting he finally gets back on the board.
The Colts might not give us much to celebrate Thursday night, but that doesn't mean we can't find a few winning tickets.

title: 3 Matchups to Watch in Colts vs. Texans Primetime Showdown
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts finally got back in the win column Sunday, but let's not pretend this team has suddenly figured things out.
At 3-7, Indianapolis is still a mess. But after snapping a five-game losing streak with a 24-22 win over Miami, the Colts have a chance to do something they haven't done in a while: string together a couple of wins.
Unfortunately, standing in their way is a Houston Texans team that's significantly better than its 3-6 record suggests.
Houston enters Thursday night's primetime showdown as a heavy favorite, and for good reason. But divisional games are weird, and under the lights, anything can happen.
Here are three matchups that could dictate Thursday night's outcome.
Houston boasts one of the NFL's most ferocious defensive fronts, ranking second in the league with 33 sacks. Will Anderson Jr. leads the charge with 10.5, and this group has made life miserable for opposing quarterbacks all season.
That's bad news for Daniel Jones, who has been downright awful recently, failing to reach 200 passing yards in four straight games. Against Miami, he completed just 11 of 22 passes for 108 yards, one touchdown, and two interceptions.
To make matters worse, Indianapolis will be without both starting offensive tackles, Bernhard Raimann and Jalen Travis.
And remember, Houston sacked Jones four times in their Week 3 meeting.
If Indianapolis can't protect its quarterback Thursday night, this Texans front could absolutely eat him alive.
If there's one thing Shane Steichen needs to prioritize Thursday, it's establishing the ground game.
Jonathan Taylor hasn't exactly looked like himself recently, rushing for just 23 yards against Jacksonville and 46 against Dallas before bouncing back with 83 against Miami.
But against this Houston front, JT can't do it alone.
Rookie Seth McGowan has quietly become one of Indianapolis' most exciting young players, averaging 5.2 yards per carry this season. Against Miami, he rushed for a career-high 77 yards and a touchdown on 12 carries.
Together, Taylor and McGowan combined for 160 rushing yards Sunday. That one-two punch gives Indianapolis its best chance to keep Houston's pass rush honest and take some pressure off Jones.
This matchup scares me more than anything else Thursday night.
Nico Collins has absolutely torched Indianapolis throughout his career, totaling 626 receiving yards in seven meetings. That's an average of 89.4 yards per game.
And unfortunately, the Colts could be without their two starting cornerbacks.
Charvarius Ward has already been ruled out for Thursday, while Sauce Gardner remains questionable with a calf injury. Meanwhile, Collins is coming off a nine-catch, 94-yard performance against Cleveland, adding another touchdown to his season total.
With Ward sidelined and Gardner's status uncertain, young corners like Justin Walley could have their hands full.
The Colts somehow found a way to beat Houston 19-17 back in Week 3, but pulling off another upset will require a much better performance than what we've seen recently.
Protect Jones, establish the run, and don't let Collins take over. Easier said than done.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Why Colts Fans Should Value TNF Matchup Over GTA VI Release
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts and Houston Texans could not have picked a worse primetime game to play in.
This AFC South matchup would be appointment viewing if both teams were in the hunt for playoff contention; however, with the Colts being 3-7 and the Texans being 3-6, there's almost no reason for non-fans to tune in.
Sure, two evenly matched teams, even if they're both subpar units compared to the rest of the league, could make for a fun time, but this time around is much, much different.
Not only does this matchup have the potential to rival the infamous 2022 Thursday Night Football showdown between the Indianapolis Colts and Denver Broncos, a game whose scores were exclusively comprised of field goals, but it comes on the same day as one of the most highly anticipated days in recent memory: the official release of Grand Theft Auto VI .
The long-awaited arrival of Rockstar Studios' most recent installment of their world-famous video game series, Grand Theft Auto (GTA), is set to be the biggest release in video game history.
This gaming series is one of the most well-known franchises to date, and there's a legitimate chance that this Thursday's AFC South matchup could be the sport's least-watched primetime game in NFL history because of it.
That may seem hyperbolic, given how the league has only continued to grow, netting unforeseen exposure in the form of an international fanbase.
Surely diehard football fans will at least throw the game in question on in the background as they navigate the new-and-improved Vice City, but it won't be enough to compete with.
Grand Theft Auto VI does have one barrier to entry that the NFL does not: being an M-rated game.
Just like moviegoing, gamers must be at least 17 years old if they want to purchase an M-rated product, according to the ESRB Ratings Guide . However, times have changed drastically.
Nowadays, video game companies are doing away with physical media and are becoming fully virtual. That means anyone can purchase an M-rated game, so long as their gaming account says they're of age.
The NFL is for all ages, and that definitely gives it an advantage, but the 13-year wait for Grand Theft Auto VI has garnered the most hype that any medium has in recent memory, so much so that news sites are predicting a net loss for the economy, given how many people are expected to call off work to be part of the once-in-a-lifetime event.
That's definitely a stretch, kind of, but it will play at least some part.
This day will potentially go down in history as the last video game to earn such hype, but when it comes to Indianapolis Colts fans, this could be the turning point that finally points them in the right direction.
With that being said, let's get into why exactly the Colts' fanbase should take a few hours to watch their team, despite the result of said game likely not mattering much in the grand scheme of things.
The Indianapolis Colts' 2026-27 season is lost. There's no denying that.
Following general manager Chris Ballard's firing, Indianapolis Colts principal owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon has traded away multiple longtime key contributors, leaving the franchise devoid of veteran talent for the first time in a long time.
Yes, the former Colts in question ultimately didn't do enough to get the job done, but they still carried some serious talent, and now Indianapolis is left with unproven pieces.
However, those young pieces in question have recently been coming into their own , and it has made the Colts' outlook all the more promising.
It's still a bleak outlook, especially considering the Colts don't have a franchise quarterback to usher in the new era with, nor do they possess a first-round pick in the upcoming draft, but the trajectory is improving with each passing week.
When it comes to their primetime matchup against the Houston Texans, both teams are missing key starters , making the overall matchup that much more uninspiring.
The Colts will be without their veteran cornerback Charvarius Ward Sr., and potentially Sauce Gardner (calf), as well as both tackles in Bernhard Raimann and Jalen Travis, against the Texans. Although this may seem like even more reason not to tune in as a Colts fan, there's reason to believe it'll help them out in the long run.
Second-year cornerback Justin Walley, aka the reigning AFC Defensive Player of the Week, will get his chance to serve as the Colts' CB1, or at least CB2. This is intriguing on its own, but couple the fact that fellow rookie Kapena Gushiken and Johnathan Edwards could get more run as well.
Furthermore, the Colts also recently designated starting linebacker Jaylon Carlies to injured reserve. Veteran linebacker and Week 1 starter Akeem Davis-Gaither also remains on injured reserve, meaning that the rookie duo of CJ Allen and Bryce Boettcher will be a starting tandem for the first time in their young careers.
Third-year offensive lineman Matt Goncalves will likely slide back out to right tackle to replace Jalen Travis, while veteran tackle Luke Tenuta is set to fill in for Bernhard Raimann as Daniel Jones' blindside protector.
Speaking of which, Daniel Jones will likely be the sole reason that some Colts fans refuse to tune in, given that he's played like the worst starting quarterback in the NFL this season (league-leading 12 interceptions), but this could very well be the beginning of something great: not only GTA's release, but Jones' inevitable demise.
Nobody should ever root for someone's failure, but the Colts are losing valuable reps with Jones manning the charge.
Colts' head coach Shane Steichen should've benched Jones weeks ago, but another unacceptable performance this week could be the final nail in the coffin that brings Anthony Richardson or Riley Leonard in to finish the season.
Regardless of how things turn out tonight, Colts fans should give their team a chance to prove they deserve their time.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Week 11 Injury Report: Colts, Texans Each Without Key Veterans for Thursday Night Football
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts and Houston Texans are preparing for an important AFC South matchup on Thursday Night Football, with both teams looking to navigate the challenges of a short week.
Injuries could play a significant role in how the divisional showdown unfolds, with plenty to keep an eye on prior to kickoff. Here's a complete look at the latest injury updates for both teams, including player designations and potential implications for the matchup.
Indianapolis Colts Final Injury Report
The biggest concern for Indianapolis heading into Thursday night's matchup is the state of its offensive line. The Colts will be without both starting tackles in Bernhard Raimann and Jalen Travis.
Raimann's absence is also significant after he exited Sunday's win over Miami with a concussion. Luke Tenuta replaced him at left tackle and is in line for another start against Houston. Matt Goncalves had to kick out from right guard to right tackle last week, where he played in college, and the Colts slotted Dalton Tucker in at guard next to him. That's likely the same route Indianapolis will take on Thursday night, especially with Charlie Heck listed as questionable.
The secondary could be facing an equally significant challenge. Charvarius Ward has been ruled out with a knee injury, while Sauce Gardner remains questionable after picking up a calf injury against the Dolphins. Gardner's availability will be one of the biggest things to monitor ahead of kickoff, particularly given the talented wide receivers on the Texans roster, mainly Nico Collins.
The absence of Jerry Tillery will further thin Indianapolis' defensive tackle rotation for the second straight week. Tillery leaves additional responsibilities for Grover Stewart, Adetomiwa Adebawore and Kevin Givens. The only defensive tackle on the practice squad is Cam Ball, an undrafted free agent who could easily get a call-up on gameday.
Anthony Gould and Luke Rhodes are both questionable, creating some uncertainty at wide receiver and long snapper, respectively. Rhodes would miss his second straight game should he be unable to go, being replaced by Jacob Bobenmoyer for the evening. Indianapolis is fairly healthy at wide receiver, but given the lack of consistent production in that group, missing any player would be a big deal, including Gould.
Ultimately, Gardner is the name to monitor between now and kickoff, as the Colts missing their top two cornerbacks would spell disaster for their defense against a passing offense that's been clicking over the last few weeks.
Houston Texans Injury Report
Houston will be without one of its most important defensive players Thursday night, as defensive end Danielle Hunter has been ruled out with a hamstring injury. Hunter has been a major part of the Texans' pass rush, and his absence should give Indianapolis' already-depleted offensive line one less player to worry about. That said, Will Anderson Jr. has already eclipsed double-digit sacks on the season, so Indianapolis' offensive line will still have their hands full.
The Texans will also be without wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr., who has been sidelined throughout the week with a hamstring injury. His absence leaves Houston without another option in its receiving corps, although Tank Dell has avoided a game designation after practicing fully all three days and is in line to play.
Running back Woody Marks and tight end Brevin Jordan were both also ruled out. Marks' absence could mean a larger workload for David Montgomery, who practiced fully throughout the week and carries no game designation after dealing with a groin injury.
Houston has three additional players listed as questionable, including cornerback Jaylin Smith, linebacker Jake Hummel and guard Wyatt Teller. Teller's availability is worth monitoring given the importance of maintaining continuity along the offensive line. Smith and Hummel could also affect Houston's defensive depth, although neither carries the same significance as Hunter's absence.
Overall, Hunter's absence is the biggest development on Houston's report, particularly given the Colts' offensive line concerns. Indianapolis will have an opportunity to take advantage of his absence, but Anderson and the rest of Houston's defensive front remain capable of creating problems.
On the other side of the football, Montgomery's availability provides some relief for a Texans offense losing Marks, while Dell avoiding a game designation is another positive development for Houston heading into the divisional matchup.

title: Colts Rookie Report: More Opportunities Arising for Several Draft Picks
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are entering the final stretch of the 2026 season, and their rookie class has experienced a variety of different developments along the way. Some players have established themselves as regular contributors, while others are still working to carve out their respective roles.
With Indianapolis looking toward the future, the remaining games will be especially important for evaluating the team's young talent. Several rookies have already taken on larger roles, providing the Colts with a better understanding of what they have moving forward.
Here's a look at how Indianapolis' rookies have performed through 10 games of the 2026 season.
CJ Allen's rookie season has taken a positive turn over the last several weeks. After dealing with injuries that limited his availability early in the year, the second-round pick has found his footing and established himself as the new leader of the Indianapolis defense, likely for years to come.
Allen has recorded 34 tackles, two tackles for loss, and two sacks across seven games (three starts). His first career start against the Jacksonville Jaguars was particularly encouraging , as he finished with a team-high 10 tackles, a tackle for loss, and his first NFL sack.
Since then, Allen has only gotten better. He followed up his performance in Jacksonville with anouther double-digit tackle performance against the Dallas Cowboys. Sunday's matchup with the Miami Dolphins proved to be his most complete yet, finishing with nine tackles, a pass defended, a game-sealing sack and an interception that was called back due to a penalty.
It took a little while for Allen to fully kick things into gear, but now that he's playing consistently, he's improving with every passing week . The Colts absolutely have found a player they can build around on defense going forward.
AJ Haulcy has had a difficult introduction to the NFL despite earning the starting strong safety job alongside Cam Bynum coming out of training camp.
The Colts' third-round pick has been a regular presence in the Indianapolis secondary, starting nine games, but his performance hasn't necessarily justified the consistent playing time. His 43.4 overall grade from Pro Football Focus ranks 96th among 100 qualified safeties.
The coverage concerns have been particularly evident, with Haulcy allowing a 137.5 passer rating when targeted and recording just one pass breakup. He's also been credited with nine missed tackles, giving him plenty of areas to address as he adjusts to the professional level.
Haulcy has shown some flashes throughout his rookie campaign, but the overall numbers paint a difficult picture. There's still plenty of time for him to acclimate to the NFL game, but the early returns on investment haven't been great for Indianapolis.
Jalen Farmer has gradually worked his way into a larger role along the Colts' offensive line after beginning his rookie season as a reserve.
The Colts' fourth-round pick out of Kentucky made his first career start against Jacksonville following the Quenton Nelson trade, and his transition hasn't been without some growing pains. Per Pro Football Focus , Farmer has yet to allow a sack, but holds a pass blocking grade of only 41.8.
Bengals on both sides of the ball in the Week 10 Team of the Week! 🐅 pic.twitter.com/6CdxXk6pTf
There have been some encouraging signs recently, though. Farmer put together his best performance of the season against Miami, earning an 83.8 overall PFF grade that ranked third among all NFL guards in Week 10, good enough to make the Pro Football Focus Team of the Week.
The Colts are still figuring out what they have in their young offensive lineman, but his recent improvement is an encouraging development as he continues adjusting to the NFL level.
Bryce Boettcher has started to earn a larger role in the Colts' linebacker rotation as the season has progressed. The fourth-round pick out of Oregon has appeared in eight games, making four starts, and has taken advantage of increased opportunities with Akeem Davis-Gaither sidelined. Boettcher recorded a season-high 12 tackles against Dallas before following that performance with seven more against Miami. His 44 total tackles are encouraging, though there is still plenty of room for development.
Boettcher has been considerably more effective against the run, earning a 53.8 run-defense grade compared to a 36.0 coverage grade. He also recorded an 87.4 run-defense grade against Miami, the highest mark among Indianapolis defenders in the game. His limitations in coverage remain an area to improve, but the rookie has shown that he can hang with the big boys.
With Davis-Gaither and Jaylon Carlies both on injured reserve for at least the next four games, more opportunities are coming Boettcher's way. If he can take advantage of the opportunity, he could have a longer-term future with the Colts than one might think.
George Gumbs Jr. has had a relatively quiet start to his NFL career, largely due to limited opportunities in a crowded Indianapolis defensive front. The fifth-round pick out of Florida was always going to be a bit of a project at first, but he has appeared in six games so far. He has yet to record a sack or make a significant impact statistically, recording only four total tackles and two quarterback pressures.
Gumbs is still a developmental piece for the Colts, and there isn't much to evaluate given his limited playing time. With several veterans ahead of him on the depth chart, his immediate opportunities may remain limited, but the remaining games should provide another chance to get the rookie some valuable experience.
Caden Curry has become one of the more intriguing developments among Indianapolis' rookie class. He's had a relatively slow start to his NFL career, but his role began to expand considerably in the middle of the season.
Curry recorded his first career sack against Dallas in Week 9, adding a fumble recovery after also recovering a fumble against Jacksonville the previous week. He's now up to 23 tackles, one sack and two fumble recoveries through 10 games.
Curry's recent production is encouraging, particularly considering how limited his opportunities were early in the season. However, his playing time took a hit against Miami following Arden Key's return from injured reserve, as the sixth-round pick played just 13 defensive snaps. The Colts have several established players ahead of him along the defensive line, but Curry has shown enough in recent weeks to warrant continued opportunities.
His development will be worth monitoring as Indianapolis evaluates its young defensive front.
Seth McGowan has arguably been the most productive offensive rookie on Indianapolis' roster this season. The seventh-round running back has steadily earned more opportunities in the Colts' backfield, proving to be a valuable complement to Jonathan Taylor.
Through 10 games, McGowan has rushed for 285 yards and two touchdowns on 55 carries, averaging an impressive 5.2 yards per attempt. He's also forced 11 missed tackles, showcasing the physical running style that has made him an effective option when given opportunities.
McGowan is coming off his best performance yet , rushing for 77 yards and a touchdown on just 12 carries in Sunday's victory over Miami. He averaged 6.4 yards per attempt and consistently made the most of his opportunities, while also setting new career highs in carries and rushing yards.
Taylor will remain the focal point of the Colts' backfield, but McGowan has done more than enough to establish himself as a promising piece of Indianapolis' future at running back.
Deion Burks hasn't had many opportunities to make an impact during his rookie season, spending much of the first half of the year buried on Indianapolis' wide receiver depth chart.
His outlook could look considerably different over the second half of the season , however.

title: Colts Film Review: Seth McGowan's Finest Rookie Performance To Date
full_text:
It's been quite some time since an Indianapolis Colts running back not named Jonathan Taylor performed well enough to warrant a film room.
For this reason and perhaps several more lamentable ones, the Colts' 2026 campaign has been full of surprises in Indianapolis.
The Indianapolis Colts' rookie running back, Seth McGowan, has been a pleasant surprise this year, going from a penciled-in backup and special teams contributor to a legitimate running mate alongside Taylor .
On Sunday, the Colts' seventh-round draft pick compiled a season-high (and thus a career-high) in both carries and yards, while also notching his second professional touchdown.
pic.twitter.com/20cseM8tOU
The Colts line up in condensed 11 personnel set and send Anthony Gould in motion, which brings Michael Taaffe down into the box.
On the snap the Colts run what looks to be duo wrap, with Ashton Dulin wrapping into the C gap to block the most dangerous man. When Taaffe and Chris Johnson fit at the same time, Dulin is left in a bind.
His solution, a valiant one I'd add, is to throw an arm out and slip/roll into Johnson, who is impeded enough to be late fitting down into the voided space.
Dulin's attempt creates the slightest hesitation from Taaffe, who tries to bring Seth McGowan down with an arm tackle.
This is an angry run from McGowan that is punctuated by a fabulous "deuce" block from Matt Goncalves who moved over to right tackle on Sunday.
pic.twitter.com/bjgKnfWNVt
The Colts go back to a duo play here that starts with good movement on the nose tackle. Jalen Farmer and Tanor Bortolini do a nice job on this "ace" block, and once McGowan spots the Mike defender coming into the fit, in this case #10 Jacob Rodriguez, he presses the playside B gap until Rodriguez commits into the line of scrimmage.
McGowan then bends the run backside and puts his head down to brace for the oncoming onslaught of the Dolphins. Luckily, the entire Colts offense joined in the effort to shove McGowan across the goal line for his second touchdown of the year.
I think if Jonathan Taylor gets this same read from the Mike, he looks to bounce the run outside to get the edge on the unblocked corner.
Plays like this demonstrate the sometimes stark contrast in running styles between the Colts' two top running backs.
pic.twitter.com/BcCLUdHJdf
This isn't world-class pass protection, but it's just enough from a rookie running back put in a tough situation.
Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley loves to run these "pick" stunts out of Double Mug alignments. Whichever way the center slides, the linebacker to the slide drops into coverage. The rest of the offensive line is then in man-up protection.
The pick stunt is designed to get big guys on little guys in pass protection. Kenneth Grant is the quintessential "big man", so when Jacob Rodriguez collides with Jalen Farmer and gets his shoulders turned, Grant is coming right off his hip into Seth McGowan.
McGowan aggressively steps up to take Rodriguez, only to be confronted with all 330 pounds of Grant alongside the other half of Rodriguez.
The rookie does a good enough job of "dying slowly" to allow Daniel Jones to get this throw off to Ashton Dulin. If he doesn't step up so aggressively at the snap, he likely gets swallowed up alongside Jones in the backfield for a sack.
pic.twitter.com/IO6e9h7PKp
First of all, as should be customary with most big runs, shoutout to the offensive line on this one.
Tanor Bortolini and Dalton Tucker work a fabulous combo on the playside 3 tech up to the Mike, where Bort seals him to create the lane.
Moreover, hats off to Jalen Farmer for getting his helmet across the backside 2i and getting just enough of him to spring this; that's a tough block.
Finally, as for the run itself, McGowan does a nice job seeing the "bang" read and then sticking his foot and getting vertical upfield before getting skinny through the hole. Once he bursts into the open field, it takes contact from several defenders to bring him down.
The rookie is a tough, between-the-tackles runner who can also stretch the defense horizontally when given the opportunity. While he's no stallion in the open field, he bounces off defenders like a bowling ball does those lane bumpers they put up for kids at the bowling alley.
In other words, he's entertaining and a bit destructive.
For as tenebrous as the Colts future looks right now, if the next general manager can find more players who fit that description, the team will be alright.

title: Colts Midseason Awards: An Unexpected MVP and Few Bright Spots
full_text:
Let's be real. The Indianapolis Colts haven't exactly given us much to celebrate through 10 games.
At 3-7, this team has been an absolute mess, and Sunday's narrow victory over Miami doesn't change that.
Still, a few young guys have stepped up, and a handful of individuals deserve some recognition.
Here are my Colts midseason awards for 2026.
Yes, we're giving the MVP award to the owner. And I don't think it's particularly close.
After the 2-4 start and an embarrassing loss to Tennessee, Irsay-Gordon fired Chris Ballard, put Ed Dodds in charge of personnel, and helped lock up budding star Adetomiwa Adebawore.
Indianapolis then traded four expiring contracts for draft capital and now holds 10 picks in 2027. For a franchise desperate for direction, those are bigger wins than anything we've seen on the field.
JT hasn't exactly lit the world on fire lately. But with 739 rushing yards and eight of the Colts' 20 touchdowns coming from him, he's quite literally the only option.
Big Q is gone, Josh Downs and Keenan Allen have been traded, and the passing attack has been brutal. Who else could you possibly give this to?
Ade has been one of the lone bright spots on this defense.
His snap count has climbed since DeForest Buckner was traded, and he hasn't missed a step. With four sacks and a new two-year, $35 million extension, he's becoming a big part of this rebuild.
On a defense allowing 27.1 points per game, the competition for this award isn't exactly fierce.
This might be the easiest award of the bunch.
The seventh-round pick is averaging 5.2 yards per carry and just put up 77 yards and a touchdown against Miami, scoring in back-to-back weeks. His running style is so different from Taylor's, and they're developing a legitimate one-two punch.
Ballard deserves credit here. This late-round pick looks like an absolute home run.
Allen hasn't played a ton, but he's making the most of his opportunities. Against Miami, he finished with nine tackles, a sack, and two tackles for loss, and he's already handling the green dot.
Justin Walley deserves some love, too. The 2025 draft pick missed last season with a torn ACL, struggled early this year, and delivered a HUGE performance against Miami, including a strip-sack that led to a Colts touchdown.
Allen gets the rookie award, but both look like legitimate pieces to build around.
After suffering a season-ending knee injury last year, Shrader opened 2026 looking like one of the NFL's best kickers.
His play has cooled down lately, but he's still made 23 of 25 field goals, including nine from 50-plus yards. On an offense struggling to score touchdowns, that kind of reliability is enormous.
These awards aren't exactly a celebration of a good season. They're a look at the few people giving Colts fans something to believe in moving forward.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Jaguars Mailbag: Travis Hunter's Award Race, The Next Moves to Make, and More
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are not just one of the best teams in football in 2026, they are also one of the most interesting. This is not always the case in the NFL, but it certainly is in Duval this season.
Interesting times have the Jaguars sitting at 7-2 before a big road matchup with the Giants, which is when we are set to see the debut of new Jaguars Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates. Add in Trevor Lawrence hitting his peak, Parker Washington's continued big plays, and Travis Hunter's rare feats, and there is a lot to like about the Jaguars right now.
We break all of this down and more in this week's Jaguars mailbag, taking questions on Hunter's award chances , Washington, and much more.
Could Travis Hunter win DPOY?
A: I like where your head is at, even if I think it would still take quite a bit. Cornerbacks do not normally win this award since it is typically reserved for edge defenders and game-wrecking interior defensive linemen. Patrick Surtain II won the award in 2024, Stephon Gilmore won it in 2019, and Charles Woodson won it in 2009. That is just three cornerbacks among the last 17 winners, which means it is a long-shot based on his position alone.
With that said, Hunter has a few things going for him. The fact he plays some offense will likely earn him some added consideration since he is the only defender elibile for the award who is also contributing on offense. Surtain had four interceptions and 11 pass breakups in his award-winning year, and Hunter is on pace to at least match that with three interceptions and seven pass deflections in nine games, so the counting stats could be there. Advanced metrics are also high on Hunter. It also helps he is one of the most popular players in the sport.
Right now, front-runners for Defensive Player of the Year include Will Anderson Jr., Fred Warner, and Jeffery Simmons. There will be a lot of great candidates, Hunter included. If he goes on a complete tear over the second-half, never say never ...
If the Jaguars need outside edge help, who would be the first FA they should look at?
A: If we are talking current free agents as of today off the street, I guess I would say Tyquan Lewis? At least in terms of who would fit the Jaguars. I do not see Leonard Floyd or Haason Reddick as good fits for what the Jaguars like to do on defense. It is slim pickings right now. If we are talking the 2027 free agents, maybe a guy like Myles Murphy?
Why do Parker Washington and BTJ play like they got freaky fridayed at some point?
A: The cool thing about Parker Washington is he has always shown flashes of being able to be this guy. He made some big catches when he was given the chance to as a rookie, then he stepped up the next year when the Jaguars faced injuries. He was also always one of the best players on the practice field. We said during the 2025 training camp that Parker Washington had the best camp of any of the receivers, and eventually the cream rose to the top.
Thomas has never really been a big contested catch guy, even if he has the frame for it. A lot of his big plays have come on vertical routes where he can run by the defense, on hole shots down the sideline, or on drag routes that allow him to get yards after the catch. This was the case for him as a prospect, too. Both are really talented players who just have really different skill-sets.
Who do you expect the Jags to let walk this offseason. Seems like one of our premier players will be gone (i predict ventrell miller will walk)
A: I think Arik Armstead and Ezra Cleveland are set to walk. I also think they will keep both Jessie Bates and Parker Washington for sure. This would leave guys like Antonio Johnson, Ventrell Miller, Davon Hamilton, and then some role player guys like Davon Godchaux, Quintin Morris, Matt Dickerson, and Jahlani Tavai. I think the Jaguars keep most of the role players and 1-2 of the big-named trio after Washington and Bates.
Do you think Jonah Monheim could supplant Robert Hainsey if he plays well? Or would that be something explored in the off-season?
A: I do not think it would be anything that would happen in 2026. Robert Hainsey is a two-time captain for the Jaguars for a reason and if he is healthy, he is going to be in the lineup. With that said, the Jaguars will need to clear cap space ahead of the 2027 offseason and it would make sense to see them use Hainsey's deal to do so entering the final year of his contract. I could very much so see this week, and perhaps the next few, be a bit of an audition for Jonah Monheim. The Jaguars' staff really does like him, and he keeps playing well when called upon.
How good has the defense looked this week and what do you expect from them Sunday?
A: We do not get to see all that much at practices during the regular season. We are out there between 10-20 minutes to see them stretch and do special teams and the start of individual drills, and then that is it. It is not like training camp or the offseason, where we see the entire practice. With that said, I expect a few takeaways against J.J. McCarthy and an improved effort against the run compared to the last two weeks.
Who would you rather potentially face in the playoffs, Denver or Houston?
A: I think Houston is the easier matchup, even with C.J. Stroud playing like a top-10 quarterback and Bo Nix playing like, well, Bo Nix. Denver's defense is the only one that has come close to stopping the Jaguars' offense all season long. I like the Jaguars' defense's chances with a second-shot against the Houston passing offense.
The jags are moving into a weaker part of the schedule moving forward. What are some signs we can look for that this is the Super Bowl caliber team we think it is, rather than a schedule merchant?
A: My question whenever resume questions come up is usually this: which teams are people saying have a strong resume? It is the NFL. All teams play some tough squads and some not-so-tough squads. The balance is rarely 50/50, but simply winning games at any rate in the NFL is important. I think seeing the Jaguars continue to play mostly mistake-free football, regardless of who the foe is, is critical. Keep the turnovers low, work on penalties, and score in the red-zone.
What's going on with Tuten ?
A: I fully expect Bhayshul Tuten to play , even with his injuries. Liam Coen has said that he feels like running backs do not need to practice as much during the week to prepare for a game, and he has been fine with Tuten getting mostly mental reps.
Hunter buzzed the Titans sideline after his INT last week, would that have been flagged by a better crew or in a bigger game? Did the Jags coaches talk to him after?
A: I do not think it had anything to do with the crew or the game. Most penalties only happen if the players involved in these scenarios carry on with the celebration longer than they should. Hunter did it just for a moment, and I doubt anyone spoke to him. The Jaguars love Travis Hunter and the juice he brings to the field.
Do the Jaguars sign Antonio Johnson or Ventrell Miller or both this offseason? Bonus question, do they try and keep D-Ham?
A: I could see it, but I could also see them having to see what the market looks like for each player. Both have been important pieces of the Jaguars' defense all season long, and the Jaguars could stand to keep two young and ascending defenders at important spots in the defense . With that said, the Jaguars have not thrown much money at linebacker, and they have spent a ton of resources on safety already. I think everything is possible.
As for Davon Hamilton, I think that is a down the road decision. I think a short deal would make sense for both sides, though I am not sure how quickly either party would really have to move on that front after his injury.
With the holiday season coming up, what are your top 3-5 holidays of the year?

title: Jaguars' Latest Salary Cap Move Could Hint at Post-Trade Deadline Plans
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- November has been ... a busy month for the Jacksonville Jaguars, to say the least.
The Jaguars are in the middle of a three-game winning streak since returning from the bye week, putting them at 7-2 and in firm lead of the AFC South. Then there was the trade deadline, with the Jaguars making blockbuster trades for defensive tackle Jordan Davis and safety Jessie Bates III, as well as adding defensive tackle Davon Godchaux.
The Jaguars' big moves saw them send over five draft picks (one first, two seconds, a fifth, and a sixth) over the next three drafts , and it also created some clear long-term implications. In the midst of all this, the Jaguars also reportedly created over $3 million in cap space by converting some of linebacker Foyesade Oluojun's salary into signing bonus.
The #Jaguars converted $3.85M of LB Foyesade Oluokun's 2026 salary into signing bonus last week, adding an additional void year, creating $3.08M of cap space. Cap Hit (Dead Cap) 2026: $14M ($27.6M) 2027: $16.6M ($10.5M) 2028: $2.86M (void)
Why would the Jaguars create cap space after the trades, and what could it mean about potential long-term plans for the Jaguars' front office? We take a few guesses below.
The Jaguars will have quite a few big decisions to make for 2027 and beyond once the 2026 season is over, though it is clear where the Jaguars' focus is right now. With that in mind, this offseason could see potentially even more movement for the Jaguars than last offseason, when they had starters leave in free agency like Travis Etienne, Devin Lloyd, and Greg Newsome.
The Jaguars again have several big names in contract years, including Bates, star wide receiver Parker Washington, and other starters like Antonio Johnson, Ventrell Miller, Arik Armstead, Ezra Cleveland, and more. With the way the Jaguars' cap situation looks for next year as of today, the Jaguars are going to likely have a similar offseason in 2027 that they did in 2026, which means limited to no activity in free agency and having to see a few players leave.
Due to the Jaguars being unlikely to be players in free agency, the only real reasons for the Jaguars to create cap space up until March is to provide flexibility for future moves, such as trades, or for extensions. With the trade deadline now over, the Jaguars' only real focus cap wise should be working on any potential deals.
The most obvious one would be for Parker Washington, who had contract talks with the Jaguars over the course of the 2025 offseason. It is clear both sides are interested in making a deal happen, and Washington could also be a strong candidate to be franchise tagged in the event that he does not get a new contract. It would make more sense for the Jaguars to sign a deal with him, of course, and the Jaguars have signed players to deals late in the season before under this regime.
Then there is Bates. It makes little sense for the Jaguars to make movement on a Bates deal now, even if the most likely scenario in trading for him was always for him to end up like Jakobi Meyers a year ago. The Jaguars traded for Meyers on Nov. 4 last season before signing him to a contract extension on Dec.18, six games into his tenure with the Jaguars. This timeline would make a lot of sense for Bates and the Jaguars a year later.
The Jaguars opening up cap space after the trades is likely to give themselves some breathing room more than anything else; according to OverTheCap, they now have over $6.33 million in cap for this season and are just under $21M in the red for 2027. Moves will have to be made, players will have to be signed, and the next few months should be just as busy off the field as it is on it.

title: Jaguars-Giants Injury Report: Bhayshul Tuten's Status Once Again Takes Top Focus
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- We are at that point of the season where injury reports closer resemble CVS receipts, and the Jaguars' Thursday injury report certainly checks that box.
The Jaguars had 11 players carry either a limited or did-not-participate designation into Thursday's practice. Some names, like center Robert Hainsey's DNP situation due to a knee injury, were expected.
But there was one change to Thursday's injury report that will trump all other names: Bhayshul Tuten, who was downgraded to a non-participant in practice after practicing in a limited fashion on Wednesday, which now creates quite the injury development to monitor before the Jaguars play the New York Giants in Week 11 on Sunday afternoon.
Tuten's status is a key one to watch any week, but especially in Week 11 when the Jaguars' running game is supposed to be pivotal against a blitz-happy Giants front that will test the Jaguars in the trenches. Tuten has played in each of the last two games despite practicing just once in those two weeks, and the Jaguars clearly did not feel like Tuten couldn't handle the bulk of the carries when he got 26 carries against the Titans on Sunday.
Jaguars head coach Liam Coen has said in recent days that he has been pleased with Tuten's performances and toughness over the last two weeks. Add this to the fact that he played the last few weeks without a full week of practice, and it is hard to imagine Tuten sitting this one out, even if his injury will now come even more into focus.
“Obviously, last year being in a supplemental role, and I thought he was tough last year in some of the runs that he had where he just would kind of get whacked pretty good, get up and continue to play," Coen said on Wednesday. "To carry the load that he took this past week with 26 carries and play the amount of snaps he played still not quite 100%. I think the guy is probably mentally and physically tougher than I would've maybe imagined in ways."
The smart bet would be to prepare for Tuten to play, but that does not mean this will not be a situation to monitor. It is such a key injury to watch in large part because the Jaguars have leaned on Tuten significantly over the course of the season. The second-year running back is arguably one of the three most important players on the offense alongside Trevor Lawrence and Parker Washington, and he has vastly outproduced the rest of the Jaguars' running back room.
This is a big one, just like each game is a big one. But unless something changes on Friday, Tuten still should be considered a key part of Sunday's game.

title: Grand Theft Contract: 6 Worst Jaguars Free-Agent Signings of GTA Era
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The wait is over, and the release date for Grand Theft Auto VI is here.
The long wait for the latest release of one of the most popular video game franchises got us thinking: who has committed grand theft on the Jaguars when it comes to free agency busts over the years? We break it down from generation to generation of the game, and of the Jaguars.
The first era of GTA began with the first game in 1997, but this was far before the Jaguars became big-money spenders in free agency like we will see down the road. As a result, we went with a unique choice for this selection: wide receiver Desmond Howaard, the former Heisman Trophy winner and No. 4 overall pick who the Jaguars landed in the 1995 expansion draft. Howard did not land any kind of big contract with the Jaguars of course, but for all of the hype he had at Michigan, he did little in his one year with the Jaguars, catching 26 passes for 276 yards and a touchdown, while not making a big impact on the return teams.
It is unfair to place Zach Wiegert here, since he did not sign a major deal with the Jaguars at the time. But, like 1995, this was not a time where the Jaguars were really throwing money around at free agents. Wiegert played for the Jaguars for four seasons and started games at both guard and tackle, but injuries kept him from being an every-week player. He was a solid piece, but the Jaguars got more out of other signings at this time.
Looking for a big-game defensive end to make plays across from Tony Brackens, the Jaguars signed Hugh Douglas to a $27 million dollar deal that he never came close to justifying. In 16 games with the Jaguars, Douglas had 3.5 sacks despite recording 37 combined sacks in the three seasons before. Douglas was a complete zero for the Jaguars, and he will long be remembered as one of the worst free agency additions in franchise history.
Jerry Porter signed a six-year, $30 million deal with the Jaguars in 2008, and then only caught 11 more passes than whoever is reading this. Porter spent one year with the Jaguars and played in 10 games, catching 11 passes for 181 yards and a touchdown. The Jaguars took a lot of swings at wide receivers in free agency over the years, but Porter might have been the worst one. He was cut by the Jaguars the next year and never played another regular-season snap in the NFL.
The Nick Foles deal ... never looked like a good idea. Like, ever. Even with the benefit of hindsight, it is a bit amazing to consider that the Jaguars watched his career and opted to pay him a four0year, $88 million dollar deal with over $50 million in gurantees. One can not fault Foles for taking the Jaguars' money after he won a Super Bowl in a few flukey starts the year before, but we can blame the Jaguars for making the most misguided quarterback decision in franchise history since, well, one year before when they extended Blake Bortles. Foles spent just one year in Jacksonville before being traded to the Chicago Bears in 2020.
Before the Jaguars knew about the value of Parker Washington , they were throwing everything against the wall to find receivers. It started with DJ Chark and Laviska Shenault before turning to Christian Kirk, Zay Jones and Calvin Ridley. Then in 2024, the Jaguars took two big swings on new faces in the receiver room with drafting Brian Thomas Jr. in the first-round and signing Buffalo Bills wide receiver Gabe Davis to a three-year, $39 million deal in March. Thomas has had so-so results, while Davis, uh, did not have as much luck.
Davis had 20 catches for 239 yards and two touchdowns in his lone season with the Jaguars, and the new regime released him the next season despite carrying a big dead money hit that the Jaguars are still paying for this season. Davis battled injuries in Jacksonville, but he is the biggest Jaguars free agency bust in some time.
