title: Several Factors Highlight Week 11 Significance for Kubiak's Raiders
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are on the road again in Week 11, traveling to face the Denver Broncos. Sunday will be the Raiders' third road game in four weeks, as they look to avoid their fourth loss in the last five weeks. Yet Sunday will mark several other notable moments.
Along with rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza starting on the road for the first time, head coach Klint Kubiak will also return to Denver as a head coach for the first time. Kubiak's father, Gary, played for the Broncos from 1983 to 1991 and served as the team's head coach from 2015 to 2016.
“Yeah, many memories. Looking forward to going back to the stadium and being a part of this game. Extremely excited for our team," Kubiak said after practice on Wednesday.
As the Raiders returned to the practice field on Thursday, their main focus was on correcting the mistakes they made in Week 11 against the Seattle Seahawks. Las Vegas hasn't played a complete game this season. It may be easier said than done, but it is far from impossible.
The Raiders have surpassed the Los Angeles Chargers within the AFC West, but still have the Broncos and Kansas City Chiefs in the way. Still, Las Vegas is ahead of schedule. A win against the Broncos on Sunday would only solidify that being the case.
Under Kubiak, the Raiders have won more games than they did all of last season. However, with all the changes Las Vegas' front office made this offseason, which included the hiring of several first-time coordinators and now starting a rookie quarterback, Kubiak has learned plenty on the fly.
“Obviously, I’ve learned how big of an operation this is, and how it takes a team to go win a football game. It's every week I’m learning new things," Kubiak said.
"But the great thing about this whole experience is surrounding yourself with excellent people, and from our personnel staff to our coaching staff to our players, I could not have come into a better situation with the type of people."
After starting his first career game last Sunday against the defending Super Bowl champions and one of the league's best defenses, Mendoza and a struggling Raiders' offense will face a Broncos defense that allows the ninth-fewest points per game in the league.
The rookie quarterback will start his career with a daunting stretch of games before the team's Week 13 Bye Week. Then, Las Vegas' schedule lightens up a bit. After sitting on the bench for the first half of his rookie season, Mendoza looks forward to the challenges the Broncos present.
“I believe getting thrown in the fire is the best way to learn, and the Seahawks and the Broncos both have considerably elite defenses. I really believe every NFL defense is elite because when you’re playing at this level, the margin for error is so small, and all the defensive coordinators are geniuses,” Mendoza said on Wednesday.
All things considered, Mendoza had a solid first start. However, as any rookie quarterback entering their second career start and his first on the road, Mendoza knows he still has plenty to clean up to give Las Vegas a chance to pull off the upset on Sunday.
Week 11 is yet another step in the long-awaited Kubiak-Mendoza era. The final seven games of the season will be pivotal to the organization's long-term future. After losing six of their last seven games, the Raiders have nothing to lose and everything to gain against the Broncos.
Las Vegas is set for another road game against a well-coached team with a formidable offense and defense. It will take a clean four quarters of football from a Raiders team that has been inconsistent this season. Sunday will be tough, but the Raiders could pull a rabbit out of a hat.
As Kubiak returns to Denver and Mendoza starts his first road game, Sunday will either be an upset win that potentially propels Las Vegas to a Wild Card berth or another loss that provides the rebuilding Raiders with another valuable source of experience.
Las Vegas is one unexpected win from going on a run.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: How Raiders Can Build on Defensive Improvements Against Broncos
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' defense has struggled this season, as Las Vegas has one of the league's toughest schedules. However, the unit had one of its best outings in weeks against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 10.
“I just thought the way that we started the game. I thought Rob [Leonard] did a really good job this week of getting our guys ready to play, getting them ready to start fast, getting turnovers, executing the game plan. There’s plenty of things that we have to do better, but I just saw, overall, as a defense, us play better football,” Klint Kubiak said earlier this week.
The Raiders' defense held the Seahawks to seven points and Jaxon Smith-Njigba to 11 yards in the first half. There were many things to like about what Las Vegas' defense did in the first half, but the game took a noticeable turn in the second half.
The Raiders' defense has allowed its fair share of explosive and costly plays this season. Many of those plays were on third-and-long and became game-defining. Only so much can be done roster-wise, as Las Vegas' defense has its limitations. Yet an adjusted mindset could help.
Along with eliminating those few but damaging plays, Las Vegas' defense must mentally and physically prepare to carry the load through the inevitable offensive lapses their offense seems to have weekly. It has been the opposite this season,
When the Raiders' defense has forced crucial stops and turnovers in the second half, only for the offense to take the field and quickly punt it or turn the ball over back to the other team, the wind gets taken out of Las Vegas' defense's sails. Although understandable, it is still problematic.
The Raiders' offense has had to cover for the defense's lapses, too, but the offense's lapses have almost always come before the defense's. This has made guessing when both units will have those lapses somewhat predictable.
No offense, defense, or team is immune to lulls during games. They're human. However, certain teams have more than others. Quietly, that has been the case for Las Vegas' offense for long stretches of several games before Week 10.
In Week 10 , Las Vegas' second-half offensive lull perfectly summed up an issue that has plagued the Raiders this season. Even with their struggling defense holding the Seahawks to seven points in the first half, the Raiders' offense punted on five of their six second-half possessions.
During that time, the Raiders' defense allowed two touchdowns as their offense sputtered. A similar instance against the Kansas City Chiefs occurred when the Raiders took points off the board in the third quarter and did not score points that quarter.
Las Vegas' defense held Kansas City to 13 points through three quarters, but allowed a long run near the end of the third quarter that set up a Chiefs score early in the fourth. The Chiefs' long run and the Seahawks' two-touchdown spurt both happened while Las Vegas' offense scored zero points.
This has been an issue for the Raiders all season. It is fair to believe the offense will likely experience a similar drought at some point during their Week 11 matchup against the Broncos. Rob Leonard will have to overprepare his defense for not just starting fast, but sustaining it.
Leonard shared his thoughts on his unit's fast start against the Seahawks. Las Vegas' defense forced and recovered a fumble on the second play of the game. The Raiders' defense forced another turnover in the second half, which helped keep Las Vegas in the game while the offense fizzled.
“I thought we went out and executed what we practiced, and the guys made the play when they were in position to make the play, and practice becomes game reality, right? So, it was nice to see that, and when they’re confident, and they started off confident, they knew what the plan was, they knew what the calls were, and they went out and executed,” Leonard said after practice on Thursday.
If the game is close, Las Vegas' defense must play well to start both halves, which is usually when the Raiders' offense struggles the most. It's fair to wonder whether the Raiders have the defensive personnel to hold up against an elite team if their offense goes cold.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Hondo’s Raiders Musings: A Huge Opportunity Awaits Mendoza
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (4-6) have an epic AFC West battle on Sunday with their rivals, the Denver Broncos (7-2), and a huge opportunity awaits them in their rookie QB's second start.
The Las Vegas Raiders are unexpectedly ahead of schedule, and with an upset win on Sunday, they could firmly find themselves in the hunt for an AFC Wild Card.
Rookie sensation Fernando Mendoza is coming off his first start and looking to improve after a great week of coaching, for his expected rookie mistakes.
On Thursday, the Raiders got some optimistic news when Brock Bowers returned to practice on a limited basis; they desperately need him to pull off an upset.
Kubiak was very verbose about how he needs to help Fernando Mendoza, and he talked about how the team can do that.
“Just coach and player working together. Just getting him into the right calls. He did a great job, and it’s always on myself to help the whole operation be better.”
Kubiak, like Tom Brady, is a film freak, and he sees the same attributes from his rookie when describing him in the film room. “Detailed, detail oriented. Asks questions. He’s a professional.”
The funny thing, or perhaps a better team good thing, is that now that Fernando is QB1, Kubiak has seen him change and step up even more. “Yeah, obviously. There’s definitely more things, more questions, more conversations that are geared to him, but he’s the same guy and still working really hard and still very coachable.”
Kubiak was raised in Denver, where his father, Gary, is an iconic member of the franchise and its history. He spoke about going home. “Yeah, many memories.
“Looking forward to going back to the stadium and being a part of this game. Extremely excited for our team.”
Kubiak doesn’t just love his father, Gary; he adores him. He reflected on being raised by his hero.
“I think more than anything, just try to be like him as a parent. I thought he did a great job with myself and my brothers, him and my mom, and I thought he was the same guy as a coach and as a dad. Demanding and fair, and he’s a stud.”
Kubiak’s players have told me numerous times that Kubiak is constantly reminding them always to be learning. I asked the head coach what he has learned about himself after his first ten games as a head coach.
“Obviously, I’ve learned how big of an operation this is, and how it takes a team to go win a football game. It's every week I’m learning new things. But the great thing about this whole experience is surrounding yourself with excellent people, and from our personnel staff to our coaching staff to our players, I could not have come into a better situation with the type of people.”
Fernando Mendoza went from the frying pan last week into the fire this week by going against two pretty elite teams. So what can Kubiak learn about his young quarterback?
“Yeah, in the NFL, every team can play. Every team has great players. So, the learning just gets accelerated when you’re doing it. Every little detail, whether you’re watching first- and second-down cut-ups, or you’re going out to practice, and you talk about a coverage that you expect, and then you give them something different, makes them progress. There’s things learned on every play, whether it’s how you execute the play or how you called it in the huddle, or it was called incorrectly in the huddle; you fix it. Every play is a learning experience.”
Class is in session for the rookie, and Kubiak talked about how he is learning and using information to grow. “Well, the proof always comes in the production on the field, so we get another week to go produce.”
Kubiak saw his team in the second half on Sunday have five straight possessions to start the second half that were simply impotent. Kubiak can’t let something like that become contagious, and he knows it.
“I think you’ve got to be better with your drive starters. Just got to be better on P-and-10, so you don’t put yourself in second-and-longs, third-and-longs.”
Ten weeks into the season, the Raiders head man is still getting asked about his anemic run game, the foundation of his offensive scheme. But don’t tell him it isn’t getting better.“Well, I do see improvement. I do. You just got to do it for four quarters. That’s the main thing that’s got to step up.”
Kubiak gave evidence of improvements he’s seen.
“I’ve seen really a lot of improvements in our halfbacks and our identification of fronts. I was very pleased with how the first half went with some of the production that we got, and then you get 20 carries in the first half, and it’s only three-and-outs in the second half, and I think you had four carries. So, you’ve got to get first downs. You’ve got to get the first down to keep earning the right to run the ball.”
Kubiak understands the other team has players getting paid a lot of money, but he won’t tolerate a lack of effort. He called it out on Sudan with more than one player and is still addressing it in practice this week.
“Yeah, it is. And when you have a couple plays, it exposes a lot of things, and it’s every phase. You always want your effort to never be in question, and that’s something that we’re going to get fixed.”
So how has the team responded to his stern reprimand? “Yes, really positive start. Good meetings this morning. Good practice, and get to go put the pads on tomorrow.”
Ian Thomas parlayed a great training camp into a successful season this year as the team’s third TE. Kubiak loves the veteran for good reason. “Yeah, Ian [Thomas] is a professional. He’s seen a lot of football. Very physical player. Really good in the pass game. Makes his plays when his opportunity comes and is a great teammate.”
The next two weeks are outdoors, in very cold cities. In Vegas, sixty degrees is considered an arctic blast, and Kubiak discussed preparing for the weather the next two weeks. “Yeah, outside of leaving a week early, you go, and you get a chance to go play outside and play in the cold and play in the snow, and those are some of the best football games, in those elements. So, we’ll be here in Vegas. We’ll be dry, and then we’ve got to get ready to go come game day.”
The Raiders had no prime-time games this year, but the NFL, impressed by their campaign, and the rookie flexed their game in Cleveland to prime time, and Kubiak addressed the change, and the honor. “I think you hit it on the head. I think we’ll think about that next week and just keep our focus on Denver.”
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: Raiders Get Major Boost Before Broncos Clash in AFC West Showdown
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders are 4-6, with a rebuilding roster, and head to the Mile High City to face the Denver Broncos (7-2) on Sunday.
Despite losing six of their last seven games, number one overall selection QB Fernando Mendoza is starting, and the Raiders are overachieving compared to expectations before the season.
Superstar TE Brock Bowers was hurt during the first half of the Raiders' loss to the Seahawks last week at Allegiant Stadium, and despite a heroic effort to keep playing that led to the Raiders leading at halftime, he sat out the second half.
With the loss of Bowers, the Raiders' offense collapsed, and their prized rookie QB, whom NFL execs loved, lost his key player.
Klint Kubiak was asked about the impact of losing his superstar tight end and, subsequently, the impact on his rookie QB.
“Yeah, when you lose one of your best players, I think that affects things. But we’ve got lots of playmakers on the field. There’s more production to be had than what we did in that second half.”
At Thursday’s practice, Bowers was back. He was limited, and while that doesn’t mean he is back for sure, when you are hoping to get him back to help your rookie QB, that is the first step, and certainly means a lot.
Andrew Janocko, the Raiders' first-year OC, said Bowers is a significant contributor to this offense earlier today.
Brock Bowers at Raiders practices moments ago pic.twitter.com/229tYLcRZr
“Yeah, I think we’re just going about our business trying to put the best plan together. Availability for players is always in constant flux, so we’re putting the best plan together based on what we know at the time.”
For Fernando Mendoza , he knows what Brock Bowers brings to the table, but he is also a leader, and he knows he can’t win with just Brock; he needs all his teammates, and he made that clear.
“Brock [Bowers] is a fantastic player. He’s an all-world player, and along with Brock, I need to get chemistry with all the targets, and even operationally with the offensive line, whether it’s Tyler [Linderbaum] getting more snaps with him, whether it’s communicating to Connor [Heyward], or whether it’s communicating to the tight ends as well."
"So, there’s so many different aspects of the offense I need to gain more chemistry with. Evidently, Brock is a very important and integral piece of our offense. However, we have so many fantastic targets and pieces to our offense that I just need to get better chemistry with everybody.”
Klint Kubiak will have more to say on Friday, but I suspect Bowers will be a game-time decision on Sunday. If that is the case, I would expect there to be a very good chance he plays.
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: Raiders Thursday Injury Report Leaves Room for Real Optimism
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders returned to the practice field on Wednesday, marking their second week with Fernando Mendoza as the team's starting quarterback. Las Vegas' Week 11 matchup against the Denver Broncos will be the first of two meetings between the two teams in a four-game stretch.
The Week 11 slate is yet another game against one of the league's best teams. Yet the divisional matchup against the Broncos is the most critical game the Raiders have played since their Week 4 divisional matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs.
In general, Las Vegas has struggled this season, but has especially struggled on the road, even in its road wins. Sunday, Denver will again test the Raiders' ability to start fast on the road.
Frankly, the Raiders don't even need to start fast; they need to not start terribly, as they have in several road games.
Las Vegas hopes Mendoza, the biggest change since their last road game, can be that spark. However, it being Mendoza's first road game will be a challenge in itself. In many ways, Mendoza will need his supporting cast to play better in Week 11.
Their Week 10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks proved they can compete for four quarters if they can not be down by double digits entering the second quarter or the second half.
Their best hope of pulling off an upset on Sunday is to avoid sleepwalking through the first half, as they have in many of their games this season. A hot start, or at least not a bad start, will be critical to Las Vegas making Week 11 competitive.
The Raiders' injury report has been fairly light over the past few weeks. However, the players listed last week were also on this Wednesday's and Thursday's injury reports.
Matt Gay, Brock Bowers, Ian Thomas, Tonka Hemingway, Thomas Booker, and Folorunso Fatukasi were listed on Wednesday's report. Booker and Thomas fully participated on Wednesday. Bowers and Hemingway missed Wednesday's practice. Gay and Fatukasi were limited.
On Thursday, Bowers and Thomas practiced on a limited basis. Booker fully participated. Hemingway,  Fatukasi, Gay, and Trey Zuhn did not practice on Thursday.
The Raiders will hit the road again in Week 11 to face the Denver Broncos in a matchup that has rarely gone their way in recent seasons. Yet the Raiders team the Broncos will meet on Sunday will be different than even the Raiders team that took the field the first 10 weeks of the season.
With Mendoza under center, Las Vegas has plenty to continue working on as they continue searching for their first win against a team with a winning record this season. The final seven games of the season will be a lead-up to what will be an extremely critical offseason for Las Vegas.
Yet at 4-6, the Raiders are a win or two from being very much in the playoff hunt this season. Wth one of the league's toughest schedules, they will have to beat a team with a winning record sooner or later. If they do make it to the playoffs, the only teams there will have winning records.
Week 11 against the Broncos is another chance for Las Vegas to pull off an upset that would give them a legitimate shot at a Wild Card spot, with several winnable games and their Bye Week on the horizon. Las Vegas' roster deficiencies will be apparent weekly; they can be overcome.
As they prepare to face the Broncos for the first time this season, they're still searching for answers at several positions they had questions about the last time they faced Denver. Although improved, Las Vegas is undoubtedly outmatched, on paper, at several positions.
The Raiders' shaky play at guard, inability to run the ball, and difficulty stopping the run all pose issues against a solid Broncos team. Wednesday was another step in the Mendoza era, which is just beginning. On paper, the Raiders have a long Sunday ahead against one of the league's best.
It will be up to Kubiak's coaching staff to lean on their ability to develop the talent that is on the roster, on both sides of the ball. Week 11 may have been against a backup quarterback, but the Raiders have shown they can consistently compete at a high level.
They have just been inconsistent in showing that consistency.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 2 Key Factors at Stake for Raiders Against Broncos
full_text:
Week 10 provided some positives and negatives for the Las Vegas Raiders, who fell to the Seattle Seahawks.
For the first time, Raider Nation had an opportunity to watch Fernando Mendoza start for the Silver and Black. The result of the game was obviously disappointing , but it's time to flush that away and move forward to this week's matchup against the Denver Broncos. It's another daunting opponent, but the Raiders need to overlook that, as they have plenty to play for. Here's what's on the line for Las Vegas in Week 11.
The AFC playoff picture is fascinating. As currently constituted, it appears the teams occupying the top seven spots are cemented, with inevitable movement among those participants. On the other hand, there's still a faint chance for the Raiders to sneak into the postseason.
At the moment, Las Vegas is two games behind the Cleveland Browns, who are currently seventh in the AFC. It goes without saying that the Raiders have an uphill battle to make the playoffs, but at this point, I would say they're the only team on the outside looking in with a chance to creep into the postseason.
The New England Patriots are technically ahead of Las Vegas in the standings, but their season is de facto over with Drake Maye potentially out for the rest of the season. The Baltimore Ravens have the same record as the Raiders, but they just fell to the once-winless Los Angeles Chargers and are without Lamar Jackson for the foreseeable future. Meanwhile, the Houston Texans squandered a 17-point lead to the Browns, falling to 3-6 on the season.
While it looks bleak for Las Vegas, it's not completely over. That said, it's a must-win game for the Raiders if they want any shot at challenging for a wildcard spot. A loss would be the final nail in the coffin for their playoff aspirations. The implications of this game are amplified, as Las Vegas takes on Cleveland in Week 12 on Sunday Night Football.
This is arguably the toughest opening two games for an incoming rookie quarterback to step into for his first career starts. Mendoza showed flashes of why he was the unanimous No. 1 overall pick in this past draft class. However, he also illustrated typical rookie mistakes, failing to identify disguised blitzes, which resulted in the signal caller being blindsided by punishing hits.
Those growing pains will remain present against the Broncos' elite defense, so fans shouldn't worry if Mendoza struggles. That said, this is another opportunity for the Raiders' future franchise quarterback to learn. Brock Bowers' status for Sunday remains up in the air. It goes without saying that if the superstar tight end is ruled out, it'll complicate matters for Mendoza and the offense.
Logan Lazarczyk is a graduate of the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in Communication Studies with an emphasis in Journalism. Logan joined our team with extensive experience, having previously written and worked for media entities such as USA Today and Union Broadcasting.

title: How Raiders Can Respond to Potential Brock Bowers Absence
full_text:
Last Sunday, during the first half against the Seattle Seahawks, Las Vegas Raiders star tight end Brock Bowers went down with an ankle injury.
Thankfully, Bowers is considered day-to-day , according to head coach Klint Kubiak. However, his status for Week 11 against the Denver Broncos remains uncertain, putting Kubiak's offense in a tough spot in a critical AFC West matchup.
Bowers is a massive part of the Raiders' offense and key to rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza's development. Fortunately, this team has a plan— a contingency, if you will— for the worst-case scenario that Bowers misses action in the next couple of weeks.
It should be duly noted that Kubiak told reporters on Wednesday that Bowers is making progress but wouldn't comment any further than he was day-to-day.
"Brock is day to day, and he’s working his tail off to get ready for the game," Kubiak said.
If the Raiders can't get Bowers ready for Sunday in Denver, fourth-year tight end Michael Mayer would be the starter, while Ian Thomas and Carter Runyon could back him up alongside fullback Connor Heyward. This group has dealt with this situation before, when Bowers missed the first two games, so the Raiders won't have to divert too much from the game plan.
Yet Bowers' elite pass-catching ability and athleticism would be a tough loss, and his presence has opened up the offense in ways we haven't seen in Las Vegas in a long time. However, Kubiak seems to have trust not just in Mayer but in his lower-string players as well, including Thomas.
"Yeah, Ian [Thomas] is a professional. He’s seen a lot of football," Kubiak said. "Very physical player. Really good in the pass game. Makes his plays when his opportunity comes and is a great teammate."
As mentioned, Bowers is an important figure for Mendoza's growth as an NFL signal-caller. The former Heisman Trophy winner called him a "fantastic" all-world player who was crucial for him to build chemistry with, alongside other key personnel like center Tyler Linderbaum and Heyward.
"So, there’s so many different aspects of the offense I need to gain more chemistry with," Mendoza explained. "Evidently, Brock is a very important and integral piece of our offense. However, we have so many fantastic targets and pieces to our offense that I just need to get better chemistry with everybody."
Once again, Thomas continues to be mentioned, which could factor into the idea that he could play a pivotal role in the game plan. After all, Thomas and Mendoza are former Hoosiers.
Furthermore, back to the game plan without Bowers, I envision an offense that could get their wide receivers more involved, especially against a Broncos team that is 7-2 despite having underwhelming units on both sides of the ball. That means Tre Tucker and Jalen Nailor could see some targets, along with Jack Bech, coinciding with more 11 personnel than we're used to this season.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. Jared graduated from UNC Asheville with a bachelor's degree in mass communications and later pursued his master's degree at UNC Charlotte. You can follow Jared Feinberg on Twitter at @JRodNFLDraft

title: Raiders Mix Up Newest Depth Chart Ahead of Broncos Showdown
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders enter their Week 11 matchup against the Denver Broncos having lost six of their past seven games. After trading Kirk Cousins shortly before the trade deadline, Las Vegas' road game against the Broncos will be Fernando Mendoza's first start on the road.
Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak explained how valuable the experience will be for Mendoza.
“In the NFL, every team can play. Every team has great players. So, the learning just gets accelerated when you’re doing it. Every little detail, whether you’re watching first-and-second down cut-ups, or you’re going out to practice and you talk about a coverage that you expect, and then you give them something different, make them progress,” Kubiak said after Wednesday’s practice.
“There’s things learned on every play, whether it’s how you execute the play or how you called it in the huddle, or it was called incorrectly in the huddle, you fix it. Every play is a learning experience.”
Mendoza and the Raiders look to learn even more from Week 11 than they did in Week 10, but with a much different outcome. Below is an analysis of the Raiders' updated depth chart.
Analysis: The final seven games of the season will largely revolve around setting Mendoza up as best as possible each week and letting the chips fall where they may, in the name of development.
Analysis: Las Vegas will look to get the ground game going, but using Jeanty's pass-catching skills may be something they choose to lean into, instead of being forced to.
Analysis: Heyward helps Las Vegas in multiple ways.
Analysis: Nailor's importance is underrated.
Analysis: Somebody has to step up.
Analysis: Miller has struggled at times this season, but is still a solid left tackle.
Analysis: Las Vegas' front office must thoroughly address both offensive guard positions this offseason.
Analysis: Backup center is likely the best position for Powers-Johnson.
Analysis: The second half of the season will be nearly as critical for Zuhn as Mendoza.
Analysis: Glaze needs improvement, but there are far bigger concerns along the offensive line.
Analysis: In general, the Raiders have to find a way to be productive on offense without Bowers.
Analysis: Crosby continues to play at a high level.
Analysis: The Raiders will need all three of these players to help stop the run on Sunday.
Analysis: Hemingway's injuries, however big or small, seem to be piling up. Yet the Raiders need him on the field.
Analysis: Las Vegas needs Paye to play better against the run.
Analysis: Dean's 10 games' worth of performances speak for themselves.
Analysis: The Raiders' offense sustaining drives helps players like Walker stay refreshed and play better for longer. Las Vegas is an improved secondary away from maximizing Walker's talents.
Analysis: It has not and likely will not show up on an injury report, but I am convinced Stokes is not healthy and has not been since before his play took a noticeable decline. Regardless, there is still plenty of season left for him to turn it around.
Analysis: These two will continue to be used interchangeably.
Analysis: If the defensive backs are getting beat anyway, it may be worth using Johnson on blitzes more often.
Analysis: Stukes plays well overall, but must avoid costly mistakes.
Analysis: The Raiders need Chinn to turn it up a notch.
Analysis: Cole had a stellar game last season when the Raiders played the Broncos in Denver. The punter single-handedly kept the Raiders in the game.
Analysis: Gay is a weapon for Kubiak's offense. At times, it may make more sense to run a safe play on third down to prevent any possible mishaps, while also setting Gay up for near-guaranteed points.
Analysis: Laube remains one of the best returnmen in the league. He usually gives Las Vegas at least one solid return a game, as well as contributions elsewhere on special teams.
Analysis: Any positive punt return is a win for Las Vegas, as the play has been rendered largely irrelevant across the league.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: How Ashton Jeanty's Production Highlights Raiders' Biggest Offensive Issue
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are set to face the Denver Broncos on the road in Week 11. The Raiders' daunting schedule will not let up any time soon. Denver will present their own set of problems for Las Vegas on Sunday. However, one problem has persisted for the Raiders.
Las Vegas has struggled to run the ball for nearly four full seasons. They have legitimately tried to address several different aspects of their ground game, from coaching to the running back position itself. The Raiders' front office has invested in the position over the past two seasons.
Yet even after wholesale changes this past offseason, the Raiders have again struggled to run the ball. It has been one of the team's biggest downfalls over the past few seasons, and it has no end in sight.
After hiring Klint Kubiak, adding several new players to the offensive line, and changing their offensive line coach, the Raiders currently average the second-fewest rushing yards in the league. They have finished two of the past three seasons with the fewest rushing yards.
As the Raiders enter their Week 11 matchup against a formidable Broncos defense, Kubiak explained that he has seen improvement from the team's running backs in multiple areas.
“I’ve seen really a lot of improvements in our half backs and our identification of fronts. I was very pleased with how the first half went with some of the production that we got, and then you get 20 carries in the first half, and it’s only three-and-outs in the second half, and I think you had four carries. So, you’ve got to get first downs. You’ve got to get the first down to keep earning the right to run the ball,” Kubiak said on Wednesday.
The Raiders average the second-fewest rushing yards in the league despite drafting two running backs in two consecutive seasons, both undeniably talented. Ashton Jeanty broke the franchise rookie record for scrimmage yards. Mike Washington has flashed his skill set multiple times.
Jeanty leads all running backs this season in receiving yards, with 417 through 10 games. He had 346 yards in his entire rookie season. Of the 417 yards he has this season, 306 have come after the catch, meaning that most of his receptions were short passes on which he did most of the work.
For the Raiders to have the second-fewest rushing yards but also have Jeanty leading all running backs in receiving yards cannot be overlooked, nor overstated. Given all of the aforementioned changes Las Vegas made in the offseason, Jeanty's numbers are telling.
The additions of Kubiak, Jeanty, Washington, Rick Dennison, and Tyler Linderbaum are not in question. Kolton Miller and  DJ Glaze could use improvement, but have been dependable this season. Las Vegas addressed the quarterback position with rookie Fernando Mendoza.
Those were not just additions; they were adequate additions. There are only a few other positions on the offense where adequate additions have yet to be made . Jeanty's stats confirm those positions likely have plenty to do with the team's struggles to run the ball.
The fact that Jeanty leads all running backs in receiving yards, and most of those yards have come after the catch, confirms he has the physical ability and explosiveness to make it at this level. I personally do not think Jeanty is fully healthy, but in open space, he continues to excel.
However, when he has to run behind an offensive line with multiple positions that haven't been sufficiently addressed, he and Washington have struggled. This isn't by happenstance, and after all the offseason moves, the sources of the issues have narrowed.
For a Raiders' running back to lead all running backs in receiving yards while the team has the second-fewest rushing yards makes it fair to believe the issues lie more elsewhere than on the running backs.
Las Vegas will have to aggressively address several other positions on both sides of the ball this offseason. However, after four seasons as one of the league's worst rushing teams, the Raiders' front office must do all it can to fix the issue this offseason and beyond then.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Inside the Mind of Mendoza: Rookie Reveals Secrets to His Progress
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (4-6) head to Denver to face the Broncos (7-2) this weekend, and expectations couldn’t be higher in the Raider Nation.
Last year, NFL executives ranked Fernando the best QB prospect of the last four NFL Drafts, and the Raiders wisely selected him No. 1 overall.
The only thing Fernando Mendoza has done is make his head coach, Klint Kubiak, look smart. The young man has shone, even in difficult times, and has earned the respect of everyone closely associated with this organization.
One of the many things that has impressed me about Fernando Mendoza is his ability to process information without ego. He didn’t disappoint today as he assessed the learning curve after his first start.
“I’m very thankful to have such an intricate and detailed coaching staff, Coach [Klint] Kubiak, Coach [Mike] Sullivan, Coach [Andrew] Janocko, and there are a lot of great improvements that I’m going to make going into next week’s game that we detailed on film, and those adjustments. I’m looking forward to getting those right.”
One thing that tipped the Raiders off to Mendoza as a viable option was that he didn’t watch film; he devoured it. That matches Tom Brady, John Spytek, and his terrific first-year head coach, Klint Kubiak.
Mendoza peeled back the curtain and took us inside that first film session after Sunday’s loss to the Seahawks.
“I would say it’s different because with Kirk [Cousins], it’s been his 15th, 16th year of a rodeo of playing games in the NFL. So, I would say it was a little bit more leaving no stone unturned, making sure we cover all the coaching points, as there can be no assumptions made because this is my first time doing this.”
Kirk Cousins didn’t even spend one year with the Raiders, but his impact was immense, and he is still helping Mendoza, even as he resurrects the Minnesota Vikings.
"It’s great. He’s awesome. He’s been a great mentor of mine, and evidently he’s in a different building, and I still lean on him, and still lean on all the great mentors that I have in this building with the coaching staff and other players and leaders on our team.”
After Sunday’s game, Fernando Mendoza told me that it was a “Dark day.” So I asked him on Wednesday if, after reviewing the film numerous times, perhaps his perspective had improved.
“I believe that every opportunity that I get to go out there and fight alongside my teammates, it’s always a beautiful day. There are some days you might not like the result, but I’m blessed by God to be able to go out there, compete with my teammates, and have the opportunity to stay healthy and get better every week.”
Nothing helps a rookie QB more than having the best tight end in football on your team. With Brock Bowers day-to-day and his status uncertain for Sunday, Mendoza talked about building chemistry with his teammates.
“Brock [Bowers] is a fantastic player. He’s an all-world player, and along with Brock, I need to get chemistry with all the targets, and even operationally with the offensive line, whether it’s Tyler [Linderbaum] getting more snaps with him, whether it’s communicating to Connor [Heyward], or whether it’s communicating to the tight ends as well."
"So, there’s so many different aspects of the offense I need to gain more chemistry with. Evidently, Brock is a very important and integral piece of our offense. However, we have so many fantastic targets and pieces to our offense that I just need to get better chemistry with everybody.”
Being a rookie is hard, but in his first start, he faced the defending world champion defense of the Seattle Seahawks, and this week, another elite defense in the Denver Broncos. Does Mendoza feel like it’s a little bit of a baptism by fire?
“I believe getting thrown in the fire is the best way to learn, and the Seahawks and the Broncos both have considerably elite defenses. I really believe every NFL defense is elite because when you’re playing at this level, the margin for error is so small, and all the defensive coordinators are geniuses."
"So, I’m honored and blessed to go against a great defensive coordinator in Coach Robbie [Rob Leonard] every single day, especially in OTAs, fall camp, and training camp. So, I believe that’s helped prepare me, and now I’m excited to embark on this journey with my teammates.”
Aidan O’Connell is a terrific young QB in his own right, and it is no surprise to those of us who know him how his character has shone and how he has helped Mendoza. The rookie talked about their relationship.
“Aidan [O’Connell] is great. He has been such an integral piece to my development, and he’s essentially been a big brother to me. He’s so awesome, and I can’t thank him enough for everything. It’s been a growing relationship, and I’m looking forward to growing that relationship even more.”
So after so much film and coaching, can Mendoza pick one thing he is looking to fix after his first start?
“Yeah, there are a lot of different points of improvement and emphasis, and I believe it’s so great how Coach [Klint] Kubiak and the entire coaching staff make it simple in a way where we want to have a focused and detailed approach on what to attack at this moment. I’m going to leave that between us, but I really appreciate their approach.”
Mendoza is a realist and a champion. Of course, he wanted to win, but that didn’t happen, so how is he feeling after that start?
“I’m glad I was able to get out there and create a little bit of a callus and be able to compete with my teammates. All of those sacks were on me. I believe the offensive line played great, and I’m excited to get back out there this next Sunday.”
For years, I have reported that one of the biggest mistakes young QBs with Mendoza's physical skills and athleticism make is that they run too quickly rather than stay in the pocket. What did Mendoza think of that part of his game?
“There were a lot of moments in the game that we reviewed after in the film, whether it’s Coach [Klint] Kubiak, Coach [Andrew] Janocko or Coach [Mike] Sullivan, they made comments on whatever the situation was, whether it was some inefficiency or a play that in the future we want to change. So, I’m taking those day by day and trying to improve on them.”
Years ago, during Matthew Stafford’s rookie season with the Detroit Lions, he, Drew Stanton, and I were talking, and when I asked Stafford about adjusting to the NFL, he told me, “It’s like drinking out of a fire hose.” A quote that I have never forgotten, and I thought highly eloquent. I asked Mendoza if it is the same for him.
“With the great coaches we have, Coach [Klint] Kubiak, Coach [Andrew] Janocko, Coach [Mike] Sullivan, I believe they’ve been able to tailor it. So, instead of drinking out of a fire hose, I’m drinking out of maybe something a little bit more manageable, and I really appreciate them doing that. However, I have a tenacity and want to compete and learn at the highest rate possible to best serve my teammates.”
It has only been one week, but even on Wednesday, Mendoza looked more comfortable. Is that maturity, preparation, or something else?
“I would say there’s so many different aspects of the game that I feel more comfortable with, and even just playing. There’s so many different variables that go into playing and what makes someone feel comfortable, whether it’s their surroundings, the playbook, the operation, and so all those things I look forward to learning and growing by, so I can become more comfortable week after week.”
Mendoza is the most famous Indiana Hoosiers football player of all time, but one of his favorite targets is his tight end, Ian Thomas, a fellow Hoosier.
“Ian [Thomas] is also a Hoosier, so that was a great point of connection when I arrived here in Las Vegas, and so we’ve been able to hit it off. We’ve been to dinner a couple times. He’s a great guy. He has a great family, and I was actually able to hit him in the game this past Sunday, and I hit him in my first game against the Patriots. So, there’s…

title: How Dolphins Edge Chop Robinson Took His Game to Another Level
full_text:
In a season that's overall disappointing for the Miami Dolphins, there might not be a more pleasant development that the performance of 2024 first-round pick Chop Robinson.
The edge defender from Penn State is playing the best football of his career, particularly in the past month or so, looking very much like the disruptive force on the defensive line the Dolphins were hoping they got with the 21st overall pick two years ago.
This is significant for the Dolphins because Robinson entered the season as a question mark in terms of being a future building block after a highly disappointing 2025 season.
While sacks aren't the end-all, be-all numbers by which to judge pass rushers, they are significant and Robinson has been on a tear in that regard over the past month with four in the past four games.
He's now got five on the season, which leads the team and has him on a pace to reach double figures for the first time in his NFL career.
Better yet, Robinson is becoming more of a factor as a run defender, the latest example coming against the Indianapolis Colts last Sunday when he fought off a blocker to meet Jonathan Taylor in the open field and then tackled him short of the first-down marker on a second-down play.
We had seen flashes from Robinson before, particularly in the second half of his rookie year when he had five of his sacks that season and 11 of his 14 quarterback hits.
What was missing was consistency and more production.
This year also started very quietly, though it didn't help that Robinson had to miss the Week 2 game against the Kansas City Chiefs because of a concussion he sustained in practice.
Robinson has just gotten better every week, though, and it might be tough to find many more impressive pass rushers around the NFL over the past month.
Head coach Jeff Hafley explained Friday before practice how Robinson has been able to take that major, and very much welcome, step forward.
"I think it's his preparation," Hafley said. "One, he's getting in the groove. You know, he didn't play consecutively early in the season. It's his preparation, and I think, like, there's nothing magical about playing well when you get a good player who starts to really learn how to practice, and I mean practice hard, like game like, and take every individual individual drill as if it's going to show up on the field, and then the jog through, and then the walk through, and then the practice.
"He's just starting to show up and understand how to practice like a very high-level player. So when it starts to happen in the game, it's no surprise. And I think he's starting to see that and feel that. And in turn, his confidence is up, right? Because he's doing it over and over and over again. So it's been a very cool process to watch him grow. And I think there's still a lot more in him as he really becomes a complete player."
With his performance these days, the big question with him just might have turned from whether he'd be part of the team's future as to when to address his contract as he becomes extension-eligible after the season along with the team's decision on his fifth-year option due by May 1.
At this point, that fifth-year option decision seems like a slam dunk, which is probably not what we would have said at the start of this season.

title: Grand Theft Contract: The 10 Worst Dolphins Deals of the GTA Era
full_text:
Since the release of Grand Theft Auto VI apparently is a very big deal, we decided to have some fun with it with Grand Theft Contract with a countdown of the top 10 worst deals the Miami Dolphins have signed since the video game's initial release in November 1997.
So, without further do, here it is.
That the Dolphins are carrying a $3.8 million cap charge for a backup quarterback who was beaten out by a rookie seventh-round pick (Quinn Ewers) is all you need to know about this flushing money down the drain.
Spoiler alert, this won't be the last QB contract we dump on. There really hadn't been anything in the first three seasons to suggest that Tannehill was a difference-maker at quarterback, so giving him a four-year, $77 million extension was silly and the Dolphins ended up eating $18.4 million of cap space in 2019 after finally giving up on him.
The Dolphins made the playoffs in that 2016 season, but it wasn't thanks to the player who had been the first overall pick 10 years earlier because Williams contributed basically nothing after signing a two-year, $17 million deal.
The one saving grade here is that the Dolphins structured Daniels' three-year, $24 million contract in such a way they're only eating $4.8 million of cap space this year, but getting just four snaps out of Daniels still is rough.
While Suh actually played pretty well for the Dolphins during his three seasons with the team, the Dolphins just gave crazy money (six years, $114 million, $60 million guaranteed) for an interior defensive lineman with good, not great pass-rushing ability.
What made this three-year, $90 million extension so bad is the Dolphins simply didn't need to do it because Hill still had two years left on his previous extension. Then again, this was the summer of "You get a contract, you get a contract, you get ..."
Byron Jones actually was a very good cornerback, but he also wasn't a difference-maker and giving him $82.5 million over five years was just a bit much.
The Dolphins ended up paying Fuller $10 million for three games and 65 offensive snaps. And this was a deal signed by a player who hadn't played more than 11 games in any of the previous four seasons, so the lack of durability maybe could have been foreseen.
Bill Parcells wanted the Dolphins to become more physical after they got pushed around by the Baltimore Ravens in the 2008 playoffs, so in came Grove on a five-year, $29 million contract. But like Fuller, Grove had battled injuries and it happened again in Miami, and he was gone before the start of his second season with Miami.
Come on, was there really a doubt about this one? The Dolphins eating $99 million of cap space between this year and next says everything that needs to be said here.

title: Examining the Dolphins Drought at Buffalo And Ranking the Close Calls
full_text:
Stop us if you've heard this one before, but the Miami Dolphins are going to be heavy underdogs when they travel to face the Buffalo Bills on Sunday, and of course they should be.
Beyond the polar opposite records of the two teams — 1-8 for the Dolphins and 8-1 for the Bills — there's also the matter of Miami not having won in Buffalo in 10 years.
December 24, 2016 is the exact date of the Dolphins' last victory in Buffalo, a 34-31 overtime decision that got Miami to the playoffs after Denver lost later that afternoon.
Since then, the Dolphins have dropped 10 straight, including a playoff game in the 2022 season.
But there have been some close calls, including three games decided by three points, one by eight points, and two more where the outcome remained in doubt until the fourth quarter.
And some of those close calls have come in games where the Dolphins were prohibitive underdogs, like they will be Sunday.
So while all logic suggests a comfortable Buffalo victory Sunday, maybe even a blowout, what's happened during the streak should give us pause — yes, even with the Dolphins down three defensive linemen.
Here then is a ranking of the Dolphins' 10 straight losses at Buffalo in terms of their performance and how closely they came to winning.
The Dolphins entered the game as 13.5-point underdogs with rookie seventh-round pick Skylar Thompson at quarterback because Tua Tagovailoa was out with a concussion and Teddy Bridgewater was out with a hand injury. Big plays on defense and a long punt return by Cedrick Wilson Jr. put the Dolphins in position to go win the game down three near midfield before the final drive stalled.
This may have been Tagovailoa's best post-extension performance and a late touchdown pass to Jaylen Waddle tied the score 27-27 before Jordan Poyer's roughness penalty on a third-and-9 penalty kept alive a game-winning drive that ended with Tyler Bass' 61-yard field goal.
On a snowy Saturday night after rough losses against the 49ers and Chargers, the Dolphins found themselves with a great opportunity tied at 29-29 when they had a first-and-10 at the Buffalo 41. But after the drive stalled, the Bills got out of a second-and-18 jam and put themselves in position for a chip-shot game-winning field goal with a DPI against cornerback Kader Kohou.
Coming in as 12-point underdogs after starting off 0-2, the Dolphins were ready to get the ball back in a 21-21 game in the fourth quarter when Zach Sieler was flagged for roughing the kicker, the first of two gigantic plays that cost Miami the game along with Tagovailoa's later interception on a first-and-10 from the Bills 21.
The Dolphins were 17-point underdogs when they went to Buffalo with an 0-5 record to face the 4-1 Bills, yet led 14-9 heading into the fourth quarter before a late collapsing that included a Preston Williams fumble inside the Miami 30. That game ended with Micah Hyde returning the Dolphins' onside kick attempt for a touchdown.
There was nothing particularly noteworthy about this game, other than it featured three interceptions by Dolphins QB Jay Cutler.
This was the week after the Dolphins hung 70 points on the Denver Broncos to get to 3-0 on the season, and the teams traded touchdowns on the first five possessions before the Bills scored 10 points in the final 3:12 of the first half to go ahead 31-14.
This was a rough day for the Miami offense, and it was encapsulated by a dreadful play near the end of the first half when the Dolphins were in position to break a 3-3 tie. This was when on a third-and-5 from the Buffalo 12 with 24 second left a shotgun snap from center Austin Reiter hit Mike Gesicki while he was in motion and the Bills recovered the fumble to end the scoring threat.
The Dolphins actually were favored in this game because the Bills already had clinched the AFC East title and they were expected to play their starters little or not at all and Miami would clinch a playoff spot with a win. The Dolphins actually led 3-0 after the first quarter, but then Josh Allen threw three touchdown passes that combined with a punt return for another score made it 28-6 at halftime. Allen was done after that, and so were the Dolphins' playoff hopes.
In what became Adam Gase's final game as Dolphins head coach, Josh Allen got his first win against Miami by passing for three touchdowns and rushing for two more as a 14-14 halftime game got out of hand.

title: Dolphins First Week 11 Injury Report: Brewer Status Quo, Punter Problem, and More
full_text:
Center Aaron Brewer missing another practice as he remains in the concussion protocol clearly was the biggest headline of the Miami Dolphins' first injury report for Week 11, but there are several other issues worth monitoring.
The most glaring ones would be at wide receiver, where injuries continue to happen, and at punter.
The situation with punter Bradley Pinion missing practice because a right groin injury maybe shouldn't have been easy to predict after the Dolphins signed punter Jack Browning to the practice squad earlier Wednesday.
As a general rule, NFL teams don't have two punters or two kickers on the team (active roster and practice squad) unless there's an injury, so the Browning move should have been a sign.
As we indicated earlier, Browning has appeared in five NFL games but none since the 2024 season and hasn't even punted in a preseason since then.
The issue at wide receiver is that rookie Caleb Douglas joined the list of injured players at that position as he was limited with a shoulder injury. There was good news there, though, with Chris Bell back at practice (albeit on a limited basis) after both he and Jared Wayne missed the game against the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday.
Wayne was among the five players who didn't practice, a group that included safety Dante Trader Jr. (shoulder/groin) and cornerback Jaylin Simpson (knee).
Trader has been battling injuries for a few weeks now and one wonders whether he'll need to be shut down at some point to allow him to get back to 100 percent.
While it's early in the week, the best projection if Trader can't play against Buffalo would be for Zayne Anderson to get the start alongside rookie Michael Taaffe even if Kyle Louis has been getting regular snaps on defense since coming off IR. Louis has been used as a type of nickel linebacker as opposed to a true safety.
Simpson is primarily a special teams contributor, and if Wayne can't play again, then it would mean another game for veteran Jalen Tolbert.
Along with the five players who didn't practice, the Dolphins had five others who were limited. Besides Bell and Douglas, there was LS Tucker Addington again (shoulder), CB JuJu Brents (neck) and C Andrew Meyer (neck).
In the event that both Brewer and Meyer wound up sidelined for the Buffalo game, then we'd be looking at Jarrett Kingston, who played center for two snaps against the Colts when Meyer briefly left the game.
The Bills also had five players sit out practice Wednesday, with guard O'Cyrus Torrence's absence related to a personal issue.
The focus for Buffalo should be in the secondary, which was missing Wednesday cornerbacks Dee Alford (concussion) and Christian Benford (groin).
Furthermore, three safeties were limited in practice, including recent acquisition Amani Hooker (knee) along with Damar Hamlin (toe) and Cole Bishop (shoulder).

title: How the Dolphins (AKA Vice City Manatees) Have Embraced GTA VI
full_text:
It's officially the day before one of the most anticipated video games of all time releases on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S: Grand Theft Auto VI. Developed by Rockstar Games, the newest entry in the series will take players back to Leonida and Vice City for the first time since 2002.
The city of Miami has embraced the game's release in a way that hasn't been seen since Los Angeles hyped up GTA V all the way back in 2013. That includes the Miami Dolphins, who have partnered with Rockstar to ensure all of Miami-Dade County is ready when the game goes live.
Something you'll find in the game is a parody of the Dolphins that has appeared on real-life signs, billboards, and art. What we know about the in-game equivalent of the Dolphins is limited, but some clues could indicate they'll be a big presence in the latest story to come out of Vice City.
Just like the Miami Heat and Miami Marlins, the Dolphins have an in-game counterpart with a similar name, but not the same because of licensing and copyright issues. The Heat are known as the Narcos (yikes), the Marlins are the Flamingos, and the Dolphins are the Manatees.
The resemblance is undeniable, with the Manatees adopting an aqua and pink color scheme, and the logo featuring a manatee rocking a VC football helmet in front of a pink and black sunbeam. They compete in the American Football Federation (AFF). If you're one of the fans who miss the era of Dolphins logos that feature the dolphin wearing the M helmet, GTA VI has you covered.
Rockstar Games has prioritized advertising fictional in-game brands out in Miami, and the Manatees are no exception. Digital signage for the team has been spotted at Bayfront Park, Miami International Airport, and the Clevelander. Manatees merchandise, including jerseys and footballs, is being sold online.
Two people can be seen wearing Manatees jerseys in the game's trailers and box art. The first is Dre'Quan Priest, who appears to be friends with the game's playable protagonists, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos. The second is the unnamed cover girl featured on the game's box art, wearing a cropped Manatees jersey over a bikini.
We don't know much about the Manatees, including whether or not they're also in a rebuild. We don't even know where they play, as Hard Rock Stadium might not be featured in the game, unlike the Kaseya Center (Sahara Arena) and loanDepot Park (Fleeca Field).
You would think the Flamingos would play at Flecca Field, but instead, it appears to be home to a second football team, the Mambas, according to banners hanging around the stadium. There's much less information about this team aside from a mention during a heist in GTA V, in which you steal a football signed by a former player, BJ Smith.
The Miami Dolphins have partnered with Rockstar Games, featuring GTA VI advertising at Hard Rock Stadium in the form of signage around the seats, video boards, and walkways leading into the stadium. It's equally hard to miss the Vice City-themed Goodyear Blimp flying over Hard Rock Stadium on game day.
From the Dolphins' perspective, the Vice City Manatees provide an opportunity for players around the world to want to become fans of the real-life team, just like the Narcos and Flamingos. Consdering GTA V sold 235 million copies worldwide and generated over $10 billion in revenue,  that's a lot of reasons to be all aboard the latest installment.
A popular trend on social media is seeing what people and teams looked like back in 2013, when GTA V was originally released on the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3. That includes the Dolphins, who debuted their new-era logo and uniforms at Sun Life Stadium that year.
This was the second season for head coach Joe Philbin in what would be known as a mediocre era for the Dolphins, as he never got the team to the playoffs or even a winning record before being fired in 2015.
Miami ended up with an 8-8 record, with their most memorable win in 2013 coming on Halloween night over Cincinnati when Cameron Wake sacked Andy Dalton in the end zone in overtime for a game-winning safety.
Quarterback Ryan Tannehill led the Dolphins to three straight wins to begin the season with an offense that featured running back Lamar Miller and wide receivers Brian Hartline and Mike Wallace. On defense, Wake and Brent Grimes were the stars, allowing only one game in which the opposing offense scored 30+ points.
Turnovers killed the Dolphins, with Tannehill throwing 17 interceptions that season. They lost six of their next eight games before a late-season run, winning three straight (including a marquee win over New England) before dropping their final two games to Buffalo and the New York Jets.
They didn't do themselves any favors in the 2013 NFL draft, trading up to take defensive end Dion Jordan with the third overall pick. They passed on offensive tackle Lane Johnson, who was selected by Philadelphia right after. He would go on to play for the Eagles for 14 seasons, becoming a six-time Pro Bowl selection and winning two Super Bowls.

title: Breaking Down the Latest Dolphins Roster Moves, with Another Win for the 2026 Draft Class
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins have made their decision on rookie edge defender Max Llewellyn, and for the moment at least want to keep him around.
That's the takeaway from the latest Dolphins roster moves, as they signed Llewellyn from the practice squad to the active roster, clearing the way for him to be able to play against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on Sunday.
In an accompanying move, the Dolphins signed punter Jack Browning to the practice squad to fill that slot. Browning has appeared in five NFL games, all with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2024 when he averaged 42.5 yards on 10 punts, with a net of 34.6 yards.
Browning has been out of the NFL since December 2024 except for a one-week stint with the Arizona Cardinals in training camp this summer.
The Dolphins, of course, have veteran Bradley Pinion to handling the punting duties and there's nothing about Browning that suggests he could be a long-term answer, so perhaps Pinion is dealing with some sort of physical issue.
Llewellyn, the seventh-round pick out of Iowa, had been on the practice squad since he was waived the day after the cuts to the 53-player limit to accommodate the eight newcomers the team brought in from the outside.
Llewelly played the maximum three games allowed as a practice squad elevation when he suited up against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 2, the New York Jets in Week 7 and the New England Patriots in Week 8.
In those three games, he got only six total snaps on defense and eight more on special teams, but clearly the Dolphins liked his potential enough to want to see him in action again.
He becomes the sixth edge defender on the 53-man roster after Eric Watts also was signed from the practice squad Tuesday.
The Dolphins are very light at the defensive tackle position with only three players — Kenneth Grant, Keith Cooper Jr., Jordan Jefferson — after placing Zeek Biggers and Jordan Phillips on IR, but Watts (6-5, 277) might be able to slide inside for a certain number of snaps and veteran Matthew Butler figures to get elevated from the practice squad for the Buffalo game.
Llewellyn was the last of the Dolphins' league-high 13 draft picks this year and all of them are with the team — 11 on the active roster, linebacker Trey Moore on injured reserve, and guard DJ Campbell on the practice squad.
After all the moves of the past two days, here's the updated 16-man Dolphins practice squad (they do not have an international player exemption at the moment):

title: Why This Dolphins Season So Far Has Been a Success ... Even Beyond Getting a High 2027 Draft Pick
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins are tied for the worst record in the NFL after starting 1-8 in Jeff Hafley's first year as head coach, and it would surprise no one if they ended up at the very bottom of the league standings by the end of the season.
But the truth is they're still having a productive season, and not just because they'll end up with one of the very first picks in the 2027 NFL draft.
See, this season never was about wins and losses, something Hafley said time and time again to make sure his message didn't get lost or expectations would start surpassing reality.
The 2026 season, once the Dolphins overhauled their roster to clear up their cap situation for a fresh financial start, became about establishing a foundation, player development and player evaluation.
With regards to those objectives, the Dolphins are winning.
NFL writer Jourdan Rodrigue put it perfectly with a comment that accompanied placing the Dolphins in Tier 1 of teams in terms of problem-solving when it comes to roster management.
"If you don’t think the 1-8 Dolphins belong in this tier in this specific exercise , you simply don’t appreciate the elegance of the line they currently walk," Rodrigue wrote. "(I will add, it has to be really tough on the players and coaches.) From a team-building perspective, they have struck a perfect balance between showcasing young talent — rookie receiver Caleb Douglas is electric, second-year running back Ollie Gordon is a blossoming star and rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez will have a long career — while not sacrificing draft positioning. Even with recent injuries to starting quarterback Malik Willis and defensive lineman Zach Sieler, getting the present group valuable experience while keeping focus on a bright future is what is important here. They have also proven to be a scrappy out, including for the talented Detroit Lions."
Because we don't like the term, we're not going to use "culture" here even though many would, but regardless of the term the one identity the Dolphins have established in terms of play style is that they will play hard.
Just check out the weekly press conferences with opposing coaches and invariably they will mention how hard the Dolphins compete. Of course, maybe they'd be saying the same thing even if it weren't true because buttering up the opponent before a game is part of the game, but it's true in this case and it's actually pretty obvious to anyone who watches the Miami games.
While there's a lack of high-end veteran talent on the team, there's absolutely nothing lacking in terms of want-to.
This is a highly engaged group, and the postgame celebration after that one win against the New York Jets, while criticized in some circles for being over the top given the team's record, showed you a group of players who really want to win for their coach.
Now, contrast that to the shot of Justin Herbert in the L.A. Chargers locker room when they were celebrating their first win after an 0-8 start Monday night, and see if you can spot the difference.
That's a team in the middle of a storm with nothing but dark clouds ahead.
The Dolphins, on the flip side, also may be in the middle of a storm but there are clear skies on the horizon.
Beyond the early positive impression Hafley has made as head coach, including the fact he has an undermanned defense ranked 10th in the NFL in total yards allowed, are the contributions of the 2026 draft class.
One of the biggest goals for this season was having the largest draft class in the NFL produce a handful of players who would become key contributors on the road back to contention, and this looks like mission accomplished nine games into their rookie year.
It obviously starts at the top of the rookie class with Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez and Caleb Douglas, with GM Jon-Eric Sullivan looking very much like he nailed his top four draft picks in his new job.
Beyond those four, safety Michael Taaffe is starting as a rookie fifth-round pick, leads the team with three interceptions, tight end Will Kacmarek should have a long NFL future as a blocking specialist, and Kyle Louis is getting more and more work as a nickel linebacker.
And that's not even mentioning Chris Bell and Trey Moore, who also could become contributors at some point.
Another goal for this season was getting a good sense of whether Malik Willis could become a long-term answer at quarterback, and that remains unsolved for a variety of factors, including how much he's limited by his supporting cast and durability concerns with him currently on IR.
Regardless, the Dolphins always were going to need to beef up the roster around the quarterback, Willis or somebody else, before they really can think about competing.
This season was about taking the first steps in the right direction, and it says here the Dolphins absolutely have done that.
It does stink that the Dolphins have such a poor record, but anybody thinking playoffs with all the personnel losses and dead cap space they were carrying was fooling himself.
The goals for 2026 simply were different. And in that respect, the Dolphins are having a perfectly fine season.

title: Poup's Perspective: Honest Assessment of Kyle McCord's Dolphins Debut
full_text:
Kyle McCord's NFL debut for the Miami Dolphins on Sunday was fine.
Nothing more, nothing less.
It was the kind of debut that told us we need to see more before forming any sort of big-picture evaluation in terms of McCord's ceiling and whether his ceiling is potential future starter, dependable backup or not even that much.
The final numbers were pedestrian, with McCord completing 17 of 32 passes for 209 yards with no touchdowns and no interceptions and a passer rating of 73.6.
More than anything, McCord showed the moment wasn't too big for him, which actually is a solid accomplishment because there have been previous quarterbacks — and we could name a couple of Dolphins examples — who clearly were overwhelmed by the moment.
Something else that was positive is the Dolphins had a chance to win the game and we could go as far as suggest they should have won the game but didn't because kicker Zane Gonzalez missed three kicks that cost the team seven points in a two-point loss.
The question, of course, is how much would McCord have had to do with the victory considering the Dolphins got a pick-six from rookie cornerback Chris Johnson and their first touchdown was a pass thrown by wide receiver Malik Washington.
To be sure, McCord was working at a disadvantage in a way because the offensive line was missing its best player, Aaron Brewer, and it might not be coincidence that the three passes batted down at the line of scrimmage came when his replacement Andrew Meyer gave ground to a defensive lineman.
That, of course, included the failed fourth-and-17 attempt for Kevin Coleman Jr. on the Dolphins' final drive.
The flip side, though, is that McCord had the benefit of going up against a bad Indianapolis defense.
This was a Colts defense a week removed from giving up 508 total yards against the Dallas Cowboys, that was missing two starting linebackers, that lost its two starting cornerbacks — and two best defensive players — to injury in the first half when Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward were injured.
So, Brewer or no Brewer, this was about as good an opportunity for a quarterback making his first start as there was.
And again, McCord was fine.
But, no, he wasn't better than Malik Willis.
The eye test should have been enough to see that, but for those who want numbers, we can try these:
-- McCord completed 53.1 percent of his passes; Willis topped that number in six of his eight starts and is at 58.2 on the season.
-- McCord's passer rating didn't match Willis' season number of 76.1, which includes figures of 130.7 and 92.1 against the Jets and Patriots before that number dropped to 50.1 against the Lions when he was visibly compromised by the groin injury that landed him on injured reserve.
-- In terms of yardage, McCord's number was higher than Willis' season average of 176.1, but Willis has four games between 208 and 220 yards.
In terms of certain analytics, there were some favoring McCord and some favoring Willis.
But one thing that was clear is the Dolphins designed a game plan to make things simpler for McCord, highlighted by a couple of screen passes that proved very effective.
In fact, McCord's first NFL completion was a short throw to fullback DJ Herman after he leaked out of the backfield that converted a third-and-7.
McCord had a couple of really nice throws, the sideline shot to Caleb Douglas, the deep middle crosser to Douglas, but he was victimized by a couple of drops and a couple of throws where his receiver simply didn't get open.
In other words, McCord was dealing with the same issues that have hampered Willis all season.
The one difference is that McCord was healthy, whereas Willis has barely spent a week without being on the injury report with one issue or another.
McCord will get at least three more shots at starting for the Dolphins before Willis is eligible to return from injured reserve, and it does look like he'll do his part and at the very least be able to manage the game.
That's the baseline that he seemed to establish with that start against the Colts, and there's no to dismiss the idea there could be more to his game because this, after all, was his first NFL appearance.
And for a first go, again, it was just fine.

title: More Bad News Amid Flurry of Dolphins Roster Moves
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins indeed went the familiar route when it came time to replenish the defensive tackle position, which took another hit Tuesday.
The team announced a series of roster moves that included Jordan Phillips joining Zeek Biggers in going on injured reserve.
The Dolphins also signed three players from their practice squad to the active roster — defensive tackle Jordan Jefferson, quarterback Brady Cook and edge Eric Watts.
Lastly, the Dolphins signed four players to the practice squad, including kicker Daniel Carlson. The others are WR Brady Boyd, DL Matthew Butler and DL Chris Smith.
The biggest shockwave of all the moves obviously involves the D-tackle position, where Phillips has joined Biggers in sustaining a season-ending injury, with ESPN's Marcel Louis-Jacques reporting Phillips will have surgery to repair a biceps tendon.
Phillips was spotted leaving Lucas Oil Stadium with his arm in a sling Sunday and was scheduled to undergo an MRI on Monday, so it always was fair to be concerned his injury also could be season-ending.
As we suggested in a story earlier Tuesday, the Dolphins replaced Phillips and Biggers with players with whom they're familiar because Butler was with the team in 2025, playing 12 games with one start, and was in training camp this summer before being released.
Because Jefferson is the only new defensive tackle on the 53-man roster, the Dolphins still have only three at that position with Kenneth Grant and Keith Cooper Jr. as the other two, so Butler seems like a logical candidate to get elevated for the game at Buffalo on Sunday considering his familiarity and experience.
Smith, the other new defensive tackle, hasn't played in an NFL game since 2024 when he made his five career appearances with the Detroit Lions after coming out of Notre Dame.
Grant now becomes the only defensive tackle of the Dolphins' projected group with Biggers and Phillips having joined Zach Sieler on injured reserve.
Thanks to those four, the Dolphins have moved up to 10th in the NFL in total defense and 10th in rushing yards allowed per carry, and those rankings figure to take a pretty big hit with the three players gone.
Watts' signing puts the Dolphins back at five edge defenders, as he joins Chop Robinson, Josh Uche, Malik Herring and Rodney McGraw.
Cook being signed to the 53 figures to be just a matter of time because he's going to be serving as the backup quarterback for at least four games while Malik Willis is on injured reserve.
Carlson, who tried out for the Dolphins a couple of weeks ago, seemed like the logical candidate after Zane Gonzalez was waived following his three misses in the 24-22 loss against the Indianapolis Colts.
The Dolphins didn't sign Gonzalez to the active roster until he exhaused his three practice squad elevations, so maybe they will use the same approach with Carlson — certainly hoping for better results.
As we indicated Tuesday, the Dolphins' field goal kicking has been a problem all season, with Miami next-to-last in the NFL in field goal percentage.
