title: The Good, Bad and Ugly: Can the Saints Do Anything Right?
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints had an opportunity to take control of the NFC South on Sunday, but instead delivered another frustrating performance that raised more questions about the direction of the franchise.
New Orleans (3-6) suffered a heartbreaking 20-17 loss to the Carolina Panthers at the Caesars Superdome, surrendering a game-winning 54-yard field goal by Ryan Fitzgerald as time expired.
Despite Carolina committing 17 penalties for 152 yards, the Saints couldn't capitalize, finishing with just 49 rushing yards, two turnovers and another disappointing offensive performance under head coach Kellen Moore .
The loss dropped New Orleans to 1-4 at home and 0-2 against NFC South opponents, leaving the Saints searching for answers as their season continues to unravel.
Here is the good, bad and ugly from Sunday's loss.
Rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson led the Saints with 11 receptions, the most since Pierre Thomas caught 12 passes against the Chicago Bears in December 2007.
After missing the first seven games of the season, the rookie wideout has wasted little time demonstrating why New Orleans selected him eighth overall in April's NFL Draft.
His separation, contested catches, and reliability complement Chris Olave and should make this passing attack even deadlier.
However, the offense has become too predictable.
After a strong performance last week, the Saints' rushing attack went back to its old ways, gaining just 49 yards on 23 carries (2.1 yards per carry) against Carolina.
Quarterback Shough led New Orleans with 25 rushing yards, while Travis Etienne Jr. (14 yards), Audric Estime (6 yards), and Alvin Kamara (4 yards, 3-yard touchdown) combined for minimal output.
Although the absence of right tackle Taliese Fuaga and center Erik McCoy provides important context, the struggles within the ground attack were already present prior to their injuries.
Moore was hired because of his success as the offensive coordinator of the Philadelphia Eagles , one that had the NFL’s top rushing offense in 2024 and propelled them to a Super Bowl victory. He must fix the run game for New Orleans to sustain drives and score consistently.
Through nine games this season, the answer has been a firm no.
Carolina repeatedly handed the Saints chances by committing 17 penalties and struggling offensively, but New Orleans failed to capitalize.
The Saints were shut out in the first half, committed two turnovers, and generated insufficient offense against a sub-.500 Panthers squad. Even after Charlie Smyth tied the game with a 55-yard field goal with 41 seconds remaining, a pass interference penalty on Kool-Aid McKinstry set up Fitzgerald's game-winning kick.
More concerning is the lack of progress under head coach Kellen Moore.
Over nine games, the Saints have struggled with offensive inconsistency, poor execution and an inability to close games. Their 3-6 record inspires little confidence, and individual flashes from Tyson, Shough, and the defense cannot mask overall failure. To make matters worse, the Saints have trailed in all but one of the 26 games that Moore has coached in as the head coach of the Saints.
With upcoming road trips to Chicago and Cincinnati followed by a home game against the Green Bay Packers , the schedule provides no relief. Instead of making a statement in the NFC South, New Orleans showed just how far it remains from contention.

title: Saints Find Another Way to Lose as Panthers Steal NFC South Victory
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints had chance after chance to build momentum and secure their first consecutive wins of the season. Instead, it was another game that left a sour taste in everyone’s mouths like tomatoes in gumbo.
Kicker Ryan Fitzgerald connected on a game-winning 54-yard field goal as time expired, lifting the Carolina Panthers to a 20-17 victory over the Saints on Sunday afternoon at the Caesars Superdome.
The loss dropped New Orleans to 3-6 under second-year head coach Kellen Moore , while Carolina improved to 4-5 and strengthened its position in the NFC South standings.
Despite overcoming a sluggish first half and taking a fourth-quarter lead, the Saints couldn't finish the job, and Carolina escaped with a crucial divisional win.
Tyler Shough went 25-for-36 for 187 yards, with a touchdown and an interception, while rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson had a breakout game, leading New Orleans with 11 receptions for 80 yards.
Running back Alvin Kamara provided the Saints' biggest offensive spark, scoring twice in the second half on a 3-yard touchdown run in the third quarter and a 4-yard touchdown catch in the fourth.
However, New Orleans struggled offensively throughout the opening two quarters, committing two turnovers and failing to score before halftime.
Shough's first interception came on the Saints' opening possession when cornerback Marco Wilson deflected his fourth-down pass intended for Chris Olave , and linebacker Devin Lloyd intercepted it.
The Saints' defense kept Carolina from capitalizing, with Carl Granderson sacking Bryce Young on fourth down near the goal line.
Another costly mistake came in the second quarter when Shough and Audric Estime mishandled a handoff, allowing Panthers linebacker Jaelan Phillips to recover the fumble.
Carolina capitalized on the turnover with a 2-yard touchdown run by Chuba Hubbard , taking a 7-0 lead into halftime.
New Orleans finally found some traction in the third quarter.
Kamara capped a nine-play, 64-yard drive with a 3-yard touchdown run, tying the game at 7-7 with 6:33 remaining in the period.
However, Fitzgerald answered with a 55-yard field goal to restore Carolina's three-point advantage entering the fourth quarter.
The Saints responded with their best offensive sequence of the afternoon.
Shough connected with Kamara on a 4-yard touchdown pass, giving New Orleans its first lead at 14-10.
That advantage proved short-lived.
Hubbard scored his second touchdown on a 1-yard run, putting Carolina back ahead 17-14 late in the fourth quarter.
New Orleans refused to go away, with kicker Charlie Smyth drilling a clutch 55-yard field goal to tie the game at 17-17.
But Young and the Panthers orchestrated one final scoring opportunity, setting up Fitzgerald's game-winning kick as time expired.
Young finished with 200 passing yards, while Hubbard rushed for 92 yards and two touchdowns on 27 carries.
For the Saints, the defeat represents another frustrating setback in a season defined by inconsistency, offensive mistakes and an inability to capitalize on opportunities.
The Saints will now prepare for a road trip to the Buckeye State to take on the Cincinnati Bengals .

I think this will be a relatively close game for the Saints.
While the defense is flawed in some areas, New Orleans arguably has the best pass rush duo in Chase Young and Carl Granderson , who are both in the top five in sacks. However, I’m still worried about its inability to stop the run, especially when the opposing team has a solid running back. Unfortunately for the Saints, Carolina has a pretty dadgum good running back in Chuba Hubbard , who has rushed for 619 yards and reached paydirt five times this season.
On top of that, the Saints’ defense will go up against a better quarterback in Bryce Young , who has thrown for 2,197 yards with 18 touchdowns and six interceptions and is the face of the fourth-best passing attack in the NFL and one that features wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan (46 receptions, 625 yards, 3 touchdowns).
The good thing for the Saints is that the Panthers aren’t the greatest defense when it comes to stopping the run as they are 28th in the league in rushing yards allowed. The Saints were able to run the ball effectively last week against the Cleveland Browns , who also had a similar issue, but execution will be key.
Can the Saints pull off the win and remain in first place? It’s definitely a possibility.
However, I cannot trust Kellen Moore’s ability to manage and put together a game plan for four quarters because Tyler Shough and the Saints have won three games despite the offensive staff’s ineptitude.
Also, add on the fact that the Saints are missing two of their starting offensive linemen on an already porous offensive line in center Erik McCoy and right tackle Taliese Fuaga , the Saints’ chances of winning decrease.

Are the Saints finally starting to find an offensive rhythm? I mean, they did score in the first quarter against Cleveland, the first time this season they've put any points in the first period column.

title: Saints Activate Travis Etienne Jr. From Injured Reserve Ahead of Panthers Game
full_text:
Running back Travis Etienne Jr. will be activated from injured reserve for the New Orleans Saints ' Sunday game against the Carolina Panthers , according to Tom Pelissero of The Ringer.
The 3-5 teams face off for sole possession of first place in the NFC South. Etienne has not played since Week 3 against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sept. 27, when he suffered a hamstring injury.
Upon returning to practice this week, Etienne fully participated by Friday and was listed as questionable.
In New Orleans, Etienne is expected to share backfield responsibilities with Audric Estime and Alvin Kamara . Estime posted a team season-high 72 rushing yards last week against the Cleveland Browns , while Kamara has recorded 157 yards with a 3.3-yard average through seven games.
The Saints rank 26th in the NFL in rushing, averaging 95.3 yards per game and 3.8 yards per attempt under head coach Kellen Moore . They will test a Panthers run defense that ranks 28th, allowing 133.4 yards per game and 4.6 yards per rush. In his three games this season before the injury, Etienne rushed for 128 yards (4.3 per carry), including 57 yards against Las Vegas, and added 11 receptions for 51 yards.
The 27-year-old running back joined New Orleans during free agency on a three-year contract after four seasons with the Jacksonville Jaguars , who selected him in the first round of the 2021 NFL Draft. Etienne topped 1,000 rushing yards in three of his four years with Jacksonville. A Louisiana native out of Jennings High School, he played at Clemson, earning All-America honors three times and twice winning ACC Offensive Player of the Year.
In additional roster adjustments, New Orleans placed defensive lineman Christen Miller on Injured Reserve. The team also promoted tackle Easton Kilty from the practice squad to the active roster and elevated kicker Charlie Smyth for Sunday's matchup with the Carolina Panthers.
Smyth stepped into the starting role following the release of Daniel Carlson and capitalized on the opportunity. The Irish kicker provided all nine of the Saints' points through three quarters in a low-scoring battle against Cleveland, going 3-for-4 on field goals with conversions from 30, 27, and 48 yards.

title: Giants Rookie Malachi Fields Is Quietly Making His Case for a Bigger Role
full_text:
New York Giants rookie receiver Malachi Fields has been an afterthought in an offense that has primarily featured tight end Isaiah Likely and receiver Malik Nabers as its main pass targets.
But of late, Fields, for whom the Giants traded back into the third round of the 2026 draft so they could select him out of Notre Dame, has been quietly making a case for a bigger piece of the pie.
The 6-foot-4, 222-pound Fields has caught 22 of 38 targets for 350 yards and one touchdown. Of that yardage, 108 yards have come after the catch, and he has also proven to be a sure-handed receiver who has yet to drop a pass.
“Not surprised at all with him,” said offensive coordinator Matt Nagy. “You all have heard me talk about him all camp. His ceiling — when we have this conversation five years from now, you’re going to think about this question you’re asking me because he’s really good.”
Nabers agreed with Nagy’s assessment.
“Just giving him the ball in space, I think he gets open pretty well,” he said. “I think he has good feet for how tall he is; he runs fast, can track the ball well.
“He gets in and out of his breaks. We’ve been seeing it on film, so I’m happy we’re giving him more opportunities to get into a rhythm and get him more plays.”
Not only has Fields been solid as a receiver, but his physicality has also shown up on tape as a downfield blocker for the running game. So one would think an expanded role might be on deck for the 23-year-old, right?
Maybe not just yet, but it’s certainly not going to be because of Fields’ performance.
“When you look at Malachi, he’s catching the football, which is your number one job as a receiver, and also making blocks and then making plays when he’s supposed to,” said Nagy.
“He’s got great talent. He does everything right. And I think that ceiling is just going to continue to get higher and higher.”
Nabers added, “As young as he is coming into this league, he’s making the most of every chance that he gets, every opportunity, so he’ll get more for sure.”

title: Matt Nagy’s Accountability Shows Harbaugh’s Giants Culture at Work
full_text:
In the old days, whatever a coach or any authority figure, for that matter, said, that’s what went, right or wrong.
That was especially true in sports, where an athlete on a team struggling to win games, in response to a question about the play-calling the coach was asking of the team, said, “Every play is designed to work.”
In the world of John Harbaugh and the New York Giants locker room, that is certainly true. Every play the coaches put into a weekly game plan is indeed designed to work. However, the difference is that every play called is designed to work only if called at the right moment.
Accountability. It’s a running theme in the Giants locker room these days under Harbaugh.
And it includes the coaches just as much as the players — look at offensive coordinator Matt Nagy, who on Thursday admitted that his play-call decision on what turned out to be a failed third-and-3 quarterback run by J.J. McCarthy that lost 2 yards at the two-minute mark in last week’s 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders left him “pissed.”
Rightfully so. After the Giants punted, the Commanders drove downfield before throwing the ultimate gut punt at their division rivals by snatching the win — and the head-to-head tiebreaker — from the NFC East-leading Giants.
Nagy didn’t just admit it publicly. He said he made it “very clear” to the players that he dropped the ball.
“That's important for them to know,” he said of his admission. “If you can't take accountability or accept responsibility in this process, you'll never gain respect and trust from your peers. And I wouldn't say that to you if I didn't believe it. But I'd also be an idiot, a fool, not an idiot, but a fool if I didn't learn from it.”
The admission was welcomed by the players, including receiver Malik Nabers, who seemed willing to forgive the coach’s screw-up.
“He's seen us run that play in practice, and he felt really good about it, but it comes down to, as players, we've got to execute the play call that's being called,” Nabers said. “No matter what in that game, we've got to do exactly what we have to do to get the first down. That's all we needed, and we'll do better next time.”
While Nagy might appreciate the understanding he received from guys like his star receiver, that hasn’t dimmed his quest to be a better play caller.
“I need to be able to learn from it, use that as a play caller, let those guys see it, feel it, and trust it,” he said.
“And then when the play is called, they believe in it, and then they make it happen. And we have a better success story than what we did last week.”

title: Giants Dennard Wilson Says LB Abdul Carter is Just Getting Started
full_text:
If the New York Giants earn a Week 11 win over the Jacksonville Jaguars at MetLife Stadium, defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson believes linebacker Abdul Carter must play an integral role in the defensive game plan.
The No. 3 overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft has been one of the Giants’ most important defenders this season. Carter has made nine starts and compiled 22 total tackles (three for loss), eight quarterback hits, two sacks, and one forced fumble.
Though his sack total has drawn some criticism, Wilson said the 23-year-old is playing at a high level.
“I think he’s played extremely well. If you watch him, he’s been extremely disruptive,” Wilson said Thursday.
“He’s making a lot of plays. The sack numbers aren’t there, but he’s affecting the game. A lot of holding calls, a lot of pressures. He’s getting the quarterback off the spot so that the sacks will come.
"We’re trying to put him in positions for him to get some touches on the quarterback, but he’s doing everything he’s supposed to do.”
Under Wilson, the Giants have adopted a pass-rush style built on blitz pressure. The unit has been much more effective with schemed pressures, thanks to Carter and fellow linebackers Kayvon Thibodeaux and Arvell Reese.
To find success Sunday, Wilson said the defense must do a better job of converting pressure, even as others may find more opportunities to take down Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence.
“We all need to do a better job of converting, especially on play-action pass on non-3rd down situations, non-pass situations. And just as a whole, as a collective, as you rush better together, they’ll have to move away from him at times if somebody else is hitting the quarterback. But I think it’s all going to come.”
What Carter lacks in sacks, he makes up for with pressure. PFF has credited the Penn State product with 28 pressures, including 20 quarterback hurries, this season.
With Lawrence ranking sixth in passing grade against the blitz, Carter’s production could swing the game.
After all, few pass rushers in the NFL combine speed and power the way Carter does. His athleticism and instincts give him the chance to be a consistent, disruptive force against opposing quarterbacks, only increasing his value to New York’s defense.
According to Wilson, the young pass rusher is just getting started.
“One thing about Abdul is this: he has high expectations,” Wilson said. “He’s doing his job to the best of his ability. And other things will happen for him. Man, you should see the guy. He works so hard in the meeting rooms, trying to understand the game plan, and he takes pride in being a disciplined football player.
“And he’s still progressing,” he added. “You look at him from last year to this year and how he’s playing, how dependable he is, how accountable he is. He’s doing the little things correctly.
“Everything else is going to take care of itself because he has that dynamic ability and that dynamic trait. It will turn on. And when it turns on, watch out.”

title: Matt Nagy Takes Blame for Giants’ Week 10 Loss
full_text:
While there are several reasons the New York Giants suffered a 24-21 Week 10 loss to the Washington Commanders, offensive coordinator Matt Nagy believes he bears the biggest share of the blame.
After New York’s defense intercepted Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels on consecutive drives late in the fourth quarter, the offense couldn’t close out the win.
With two minutes remaining, Nagy called a quarterback sweep for J.J. McCarthy on third-and-3. The play resulted in a two-yard loss and a punt. On the Commanders’ next possession, they drove 71 yards in three plays for the game-winning touchdown.
Before the Giants’ Week 11 showdown with the Jacksonville Jaguars , Nagy said he needed to take accountability for his role in the loss.
“I’m pissed at myself for that play call, just to be real, put it out there,” Nagy said on Thursday.
“I’m angry about that, and I know I can be better with that call. Now, have we practiced it a lot? Yeah, we have. But in that moment, too, there’s that balance of how aggressive we want to be versus conservative.”
The Giants opened their final drive with a 21-yard completion from McCarthy to receiver Malachi Fields, but they couldn’t complete the comeback. While trying to find top wideout Malik Nabers down the middle, McCarthy threw an interception to Commanders defender Rasul Douglas, sealing Washington’s win.
If the Giants want to strengthen their NFC East lead Sunday against Jacksonville, Nagy knows both his scheme and his players’ execution must be better.
“There’s no reason why we should lose that game after what our defense did with those two interceptions,” he continued.
“We need to end the game as an offense, and it starts with me making the right call in the right situation. So, I want to make sure I take that accountability with the guys. They know that, but they’re also going to understand and feel that moving forward. That’s going to be real.”
“I made it very clear,” he added. “And that’s important for them to know. I mean, when you look at all these plays, it’s not just that third-and-three play. There are other plays throughout the game where sometimes a play doesn’t work, and it might be off here or there for a player, or it might be just a bad play call.
“But if you can’t take accountability or accept responsibility in this process, you’ll never gain respect and trust from your peers. I’d also be a fool if I didn’t learn from it.”
With plenty of offensive weapons, Nagy still faces a tough task against a formidable Jaguars defense. Jacksonville boasts the NFL’s second-best scoring defense, allowing 16.0 points per game.
While Nagy may be tempted to lean on his most productive pass-catchers, he realizes that New York’s entire arsenal of plays must be available. Despite much-improved efficiency, the Giants’ offense has struggled to close out games with the ball. For Nagy, this week presents the opportunity to prove he has learned from his mistakes.
“I need to be able to learn from it, use that as a play caller, let those guys see it, feel it, and trust it. And then when the play is called, they believe in it, and then they make it happen. And we have a better success story than what we did last week,” Nagy said.
“Good football teams live in a four-minute offense, and that’s what we want to be,” he added. “We do not want to be a two-minute team at the end of the game losing. We need to be a four-minute team that is really good. That’s what Super Bowl championship teams do.”

title: Six Worst Free-Agent Signings in Giants History Since GTA’s Debut
full_text:
Happy Grand Theft Auto VI day! The game video-game enthusiasts have waited seemingly forever for is finally here, and scores of fans are surely enjoying the new release.
In honor of GTA VI’s release day, we’re looking back at six of the most disappointing free-agent signings (new players, not re-signings) in New York Giants history since 1997, when GTA first debuted.
Arrington was the second overall pick in the 2000 draft by Washington after a stellar career at Penn State.
A three-time Pro Bowler, he saw his star begin to fade in 2004 after a knee injury limited him to four games. That, plus his struggles to fit into Washington’s scheme, led Arrington to forfeit $4.4 million in bonuses to hit free agency.
The Giants, meanwhile, were looking to add to a linebacker unit that included Antonio Pierce (another former Washington player) and Carlos Emmons. While the total value of his contract was eye-watering, it was heavily loaded with incentives.
Arrington, however, never reached any of them. He suffered a season-ending Achilles injury six games into his first (and only) season with the Giants. The following offseason, after general manager Ernie Accorsi retired, new general manager Jerry Reese released Arrington from his contract.
The Giants thought they were getting a steal when they signed former Jacksonville Jaguars linebacker J.T. Thomas, who could play all three linebacker positions .
Thomas played 12 games in 2015 and recorded 46 tackles, but New York got only three more games out of him thanks to injuries piling up.
Thomas had an ankle ailment that landed him on IR late in 2015, a season-ending knee injury in Week 1 of 2016, and a Week 2 groin injury that put him on IR in September 2017 and eventually led to an injury settlement.
The signing of Nate Solder from the New England Patriots was, in retrospect, a knee-jerk reaction to Ereck Flowers failing to materialize as the team’s long-term left tackle.
The Giants made Solder the highest-paid offensive lineman at the time, but he battled injuries, saw a decline in his skills, and struggled in pass protection. He also opted out of the 2020 season because of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Per PFF , Solder allowed 125 pressures and 24 sacks in three seasons with the Giants (2018-2019, 2021). His contract was voided on February 16, 2022, and Andrew Thomas replaced him at left tackle.
Golden Tate was supposed to quell concerns after the team traded Odell Beckham Jr. to the Cleveland Browns. He came to New York with a reputation as a yards-after-catch master, recording at least 500 yards after the catch in five straight seasons (2013 through 2017) for Seattle and Detroit.
Unfortunately, he didn’t have the same kind of production for the Giants. His tenure began with a four-game suspension in 2019 for violating the league’s policy on performance-enhancing substances; the ban resulted from a prescribed fertility medication that contained a banned ingredient.
Tate caught only 84 passes for 1,064 yards and eight touchdowns in two seasons with the Giants before becoming a cap casualty after the 2020 season.
Desperate for a WR1 for starting quarterback Daniel Jones, the Giants took another swing in free agency by signing 6-foot-4, 213-pound receiver Kenny Golladay to a four-year deal.
He was coming off a major season-ending hip injury suffered the year prior with the Detroit Lions. Satisfied with the medical check, then-Giants general manager Dave Gettleman went ahead with the deal.
In return, Golladay appeared in just 26 games with 18 starts for the Giants, catching 43 passes for 602 yards and one touchdown.
He also failed to endear himself to the organization when he openly voiced frustration over his role in the offense, starting in Week 2 of the 2021 season, when he was caught on camera having a heated discussion with Jones on the sideline.
He was released on March 15, 2023, the first day of the new league year.
The Giants were excited to land Rudolph, a big-bodied tight end whose specialty was red-zone play. However, the acquisition took a weird turn when it was discovered after his physical that he needed foot surgery.
Rather than adjust Rudolph’s contract to include playing-time incentives, then-general manager Dave Gettleman revealed that doctors had signed off on the physical and that the team intended to honor the original deal because, “We are the Giants, we’re going to do everything with class.”
Rudolph appeared in 16 games with 13 starts. He finished with 26 receptions for 257 yards and one touchdown, hardly the production the Giants hoped for when they signed him.

title: Behind Enemy Lines: Jaguars Insider Previews Giants-Jags Matchup
full_text:
We step behind enemy lines this week by checking in with Jacksonville Jaguars On SI site publisher John Shipley, who offers insight into the key matchups and intangibles to watch when the New York Giants host the Jaguars.
JS: There are several reasons. He has a group of pass-catchers in Jakobi Meyers, Parker Washington and Brenton Strange who all thrive at beating zone coverage thanks to their ability to find soft spots in zones and work the middle of the field.
Liam Coen’s scheme also gives Lawrence and the passing game plenty of open looks against zone coverage, thanks to the balance they play with on offense and how they scheme open wide receivers.
But most importantly, it comes down to how Lawrence is playing. He is confident in everything he is doing before and after the snap, far more confident than he has looked in past years.
He knows where the ball is going, and he knows how to fit it in there regardless of how open or tight the passing windows are.
JS: It will likely impact communication. The Jaguars’ offense has had some communication issues on the road this year, whether in Denver in Week 2 or in London in Weeks 5-6.
That said, this might not be the crushing loss many outside Jacksonville believe it is. Hainsey has been the Jaguars’ fifth-best offensive lineman this season, and a lot of his value comes pre-snap.
There is a real chance the Jaguars could see stronger play from second-year center Jonah Monheim, whom the staff rates extremely highly and who has played well in spot starts for Hainsey in the past.
JS: When it comes to the Jaguars’ defense vs. the Giants’ offense, the biggest matchup I am going to be watching is Malik Nabers against Travis Hunter.
Hunter has been a true shutdown No. 1 cornerback this season, even beyond his amazing athletic feats on his interceptions. He is the only Jaguars cornerback who can really run with Nabers, and I am fascinated to see these two battle downfield.
The Jaguars don’t have their cornerbacks following receivers, but this might be the week to consider it.
As for the Jaguars’ offense vs. the Giants’ defense, I am going with Walker Little against Abdul Carter.
Little has played well for the Jaguars since stepping in as the starting left tackle a month ago due to injuries, but a player on Carter’s level hasn’t tested him.
Little has proven he can get the job done week in and week out, but this week will be about proving that he can handle playing a blue-chip talent, which is exactly what he will need to do during a critical playoff run.
JS: Anthony Campanile. The Jaguars’ defensive coordinator is a genius, turning one of the NFL’s worst defenses into a powerhouse over the last two years.
They are not flawless, since they still give up some explosive plays, and they do not get a ton of sacks.
But Campanile has built one of the best run defenses in the NFL, and his philosophy of forcing quarterbacks to get the ball out of their hands quickly has led to plenty of takeaways and big plays.
Campanile should be a future head coach, and the proof is in the pudding: he has helped elevate and evolve the Jaguars’ defense over the past two years.
JS: I don’t think the Jaguars have a blowout this week, even though I believe they are firmly the better team.
The Giants have fought hard week in and week out under John Harbaugh, and I think there is a real chance they take the fight to the Jaguars in the trenches.
I think Trevor Lawrence will still be taking snaps in the fourth quarter this week, which has not been a given most weeks.
There is a lot more respect in the Jaguars’ building right now than there was the last time these two teams played in 2022.

title: Harbaugh Respects Jaguars’ 7-2 Record but Not the Backstory
full_text:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh isn’t interested in how the Jacksonville Jaguars got to where they are. He only cares about the team standing in front of him on Sunday.
“I don’t care. I couldn’t care less,” Harbaugh quickly said when asked what’s helped the 7-2 Jaguars get to the “next level” of play.
“That sort of analysis about why they’re where they are, we don’t even look at that. All you do is look at the team they are right now, the opponent that we’re facing.”
Although his response came off as rather brusque, it wasn’t meant to be disrespectful so much as to prove a point.
That point is that the Giants aren’t interested in the history of how the Jaguars have built themselves into a powerhouse team. Instead, they’re focused on what kind of challenge the Jaguars will pose when the two teams square off Sunday at MetLife Stadium in a nationally televised game.
When pressed for a follow-up on what has made the Jaguars so good, Harbaugh said, “They do a lot of good stuff. They play good defense, offense and special teams. They’ve got a really good quarterback (Trevor Lawrence).
“They’ve got talented players on offense. Their offensive line is big and strong. I mean, we could go on here for a while. You want me to keep going? They’re really good.”
Indeed. The Jaguars’ offense is averaging 358.9 yards per game, ninth in the NFL. Their running game is ranked 12th (117.8 yards/game), their passing game 11th (241.1 yards/game), and they have averaged 29.9 points per game, fourth in the league.
Defensively, the Jaguars have been even better. They have the league’s ninth-best overall defense (319.2 yards/game), the sixth-best run defense (91 yards/game) and the 19th-best pass defense (228.2 yards/game).
The Jaguars have a +125-point margin over their opponents, the best mark in the league, and have averaged nearly two touchdowns more than their opponents per game.
As Harbaugh said, the Jaguars do a lot of good stuff.
“What’s their record?” Harbaugh asked, before quickly answering his own rhetorical question. “I think that makes them good. What did (former Giants Hall of Fame head coach) Bill Parcells say? ‘You are what your record says you are.’ So the Jaguars are really good. Their record says so.”
The Giants (5-3-1), who sit atop the NFC East and have their sights firmly on earning their first postseason berth since 2022, are looking to get off on the right foot as they enter the toughest part of their 2026 schedule starting Sunday.

title: J.J. McCarthy Focused on Red-Zone Execution as Giants Prep for Stingy Jaguars Defense
full_text:
New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy was determined to make the most of his extra time as he prepared for his team’s Week 11 showdown with the Jacksonville Jaguars .
With Big Blue last playing on Nov. 12, a game in which they suffered a 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders, McCarthy knew the few additional days between games would be best used to learn as much as possible about his next opponent.
Fortunately for the Giants, their 23-year-old starting quarterback appears rested and ready to compete against one of the NFL’s top teams this season.
“Definitely get a jump start on Jacksonville,” McCarthy said. “They have a lot of stuff in right now. A lot of different fronts, a lot of different coverages that are associated with certain fronts and personnel.
“Just making sure I really keep dialing in on the opponents every week,” he added. “It’s also about understanding our scheme like the back of my hand.”
McCarthy’s concern regarding Jacksonville’s defense is warranted. The Jaguars are among the league’s best preventive units, ranking second in scoring defense, fourth in EPA/play and seventh in success rate.
Under both head coach Liam Coen and defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile, the Jags excel in the red zone. Their defense ranks fifth-best in defensive red-zone touchdown rate (43.5%) and No. 1 in forced red-zone turnovers, with five.
Given Jacksonville’s penchant for playing a “bend-don’t-break” style, McCarthy knows he must be ready to lead his team into the end zone from inside the 20. If the Giants struggle to do so, they may find themselves in an early deficit on Sunday afternoon at MetLife Stadium.
“It definitely brings a level of urgency and attention to detail that you go into every single week,” McCarthy said.
“But, when it comes to games in late November when you’re getting closer and closer to playoffs, the attention to detail, the urgency to really make sure you’re doing your one-eleventh on every single play means the most, and especially against great teams like Jacksonville.”
While several factors contributed to New York’s Week 10 loss to the Commanders, McCarthy ultimately sealed the club’s fate when attempting to find receiver Malik Nabers deep over the middle with just over 30 seconds remaining in the game. Commanders defender Rasul Douglas intercepted his pass to preserve the win for Washington.
Despite the bitter taste left by the game’s closing moments, McCarthy took some positives from Week 10. The former Michigan Wolverine threw for a career-high 293 yards while completing 64% of his passes in his first home start for New York since being traded from the Minnesota Vikings on Sept. 28.
Though he hopes to accentuate the positives against the Jags this Sunday, the Giants’ starter knows he must recognize his mistakes and apply the lessons he has learned to return to playing winning football with Big Blue.
“Winning the game is the number one thing,” McCarthy said. “There’s a bunch of stats, traits, and how a quarterback would play that would contribute to winning the game, and that’s all about decision-making, timing, accuracy, and just being smart, and knowing that you have the program in your hands every single play when you touch that ball and making the best decisions possible.
“That’s the number one thing I think makes winning football,” he said. “And I try to do that to the best of my ability every single week.”

title: Why John Harbaugh Isn’t Worried About Abdul Carter’s Low Sack Number
full_text:
An old saying, attributed to author Aaron Levenstein , goes, “Statistics are like bikinis; what they reveal is suggestive, but what they conceal is vital.”
No one knows that better than New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh and outside linebacker Abdul Carter.
At first glance, Carter, in his second NFL season, is having an “off year” in terms of his pass-rushing game. The 23-year-old outside linebacker has recorded just 2.0 sacks in nine games, half of what he finished with last season in 17 games (nine starts).
His tackle total is also down, with Carter having just 22 tackles versus the 43 he had as a rookie.
Other metrics suggest Carter is just as productive as ever, including ESPN’s pass-rush win rate, where he ranks second (29%) behind Miami Dolphins linebacker Chop Robinson, and his 17 quick pass pressures (under 2.5 seconds), ninth-best in the league.
But to Harbaugh, the rush of numbers that, depending on one’s perspective, either confirms that Carter is making an impact or contradicts the notion means nothing.
“I don’t really look at the metrics personally every week. I don’t go through all those stats and try to dig out every little metric on every guy. We get a general accounting of it,” Harbaugh said.
“I definitely look at the team stats. But I’m looking at the tape. I’m grading every single guy. Plus, every coach is grading their position all the time. And he’s grading out really well on my sheet; I can tell you that, and the coaches’ sheet.”
Carter’s lack of numbers could be largely due to the absence of fellow outside linebacker Brian Burns, who was lost for the season due to an ACL injury back in Week 3. Since then, Carter has undoubtedly drawn more attention in the form of chips and double teams by opponents looking to slow him down.
As a result of the extra attention he receives, Carter is in fact opening up other opportunities for his teammates to swoop in and make plays.
As for the sacks, which Harbaugh didn’t dispute are important, they’ll come when they come.
“He’s a disruptive guy. I promise you they’re accounting for him,” Harbaugh said. “You’ve got to go play football. I mean, you can have a bunch of sacks and still not be playing that well. We’ve seen that before too.
“So he’s that kind of player. He’s a disruptive player. He’s a game changer, game wrecker, and I think there’s going to be a lot of game wrecks in his future.”

title: Faria: Jets' End-of-Year Plans to Tank (or Not) Likely Won't Make a Difference
full_text:
It is as if Shakespeare has taken over the NFL now that the playoff picture is becoming clearer.
To tank or not to tank? That is the question.
For the Jets, the team won't even accept the question for the remainder of the season. Despite their 2-8 start to the year , Gang Green has focused heavily on trying to win as many games as possible down the stretch.
"I don't think anybody in this business is here to lose," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said. "I don't think anybody in this business can stomach just going out there and trying to lose; that's just not the way that we're built... regardless of the record."
Glenn and the players may believe in focusing on winning games, but is that the best thing for the franchise in the long run? What benefits does trying to win games down the stretch bring to the Jets and to a head coach who is seemingly in the hot seat ?
What if I told you none of it really matters—including the team's decision to not tank in the first place.
Jets fans may want the team to try to lose, but that's just not the reality of what the organization is going to do. That is the danger of trying to do everything in their power to keep their coaching staff forto a third season at the helm. The focus isn't on the future success of the organization; it's about the immediate success.
In fact, very few cases in NFL history show teams actually tanking. Most bad teams are simply bad enough to lose and get high picks—especially with seven games left in the season. For Jets fans to want the team to tank, that is simply not what they are going to do.
However, it might not actually matter.
The Jets' coaching staff has struggled all season. It hasn't mattered whether it's against top competition like the Chiefs or against the one-win Dolphins. The Jets seemingly can't get out of their own way when it comes to winning games.
Because of that reality, who is to say the team needs to tank in order to get a top pick?
New York is seventh-worst in the league in points, 10th-worst in points allowed, and third-worst against the run. As of Week 11, the Jets haven't scored a touchdown in nine quarters, thanks to their coaching staff being comfortable with kicking field goals after failed red zone attempts. The talent increase seen across the roster hasn't mattered. The upgrade at quarterback hasn't mattered.
So what will suddenly be fixed down the stretch? Will those numbers magically improve against the Chargers or the Dolphins?
It's fair for fans to want the team to lose games down the stretch in order to secure a top draft pick in April, but that's not what the organization is going to set out to do at this point.
With how poorly they have played this season, making an effort to tank may not matter at all.

title: Potential Kevin O'Connell Trade Would Be a Colossal Jets Mistake Waiting to Happen
full_text:
As the Jets look to turn the page from an injury-riddled 31-12 loss to the Bills last Sunday and try to get their season back on track amid a five-game losing streak, there are still a lot of areas of concern that need to be improved on ahead of a Week 11 road trip to face the 1-8 Chargers.
While New York's upcoming opponents, the Chargers and Dolphins, have a combined 2-16 record and should present some favorable opportunities before a Week 13 bye, the problems on this team run much deeper than the surface , especially for head coach Aaron Glenn.
With a 5-22 record as Jets HC and a dismal 0-9 mark against AFC East opponents, Glenn has failed to get it done in Gotham and it should only be a matter of time until Gang Green decides to move on . Although there are multiple ways for the Jets to go for their next HC when that time comes, ESPN 's Rich Cimini suggested that Vikings HC Kevin O'Connell could be a "name to watch."
"The name I would watch for is KOC, Kevin O'Connell," Cimini said (h/t Jets Collective). "I was just talking to a couple of people in the league today, and they said they could see (Jets general manager Darren) Mougey giving up a high draft pick for Kevin O'Connell. They went to college together; they have maintained a relationship. If something falls apart there in Minnesota, if they collapse down the stretch, or if they decide that they want to elevate (Vikings defensive coordinator Brian) Flores instead of losing him to another team, maybe they make that move."
. @RichCimini said the "name to watch" for the #Jets in the 2027 search is #Vikings HC Kevin O'Connell. “The name I would watch for is KOC, Kevin O’Connell. I was just talking to a couple of people in the league today, and they said they could see [Darren] Mougey giving up a high… pic.twitter.com/i1wNAcrG8p
While O'Connell has a solid 50-27 record (.649) as a HC and has long been heralded as a quarterback whisperer, he is still 0-2 in the playoffs and may be someone the Jets want to consider carefully.
After all, with three first-round draft picks, they could land a top-five talent at QB amid the injury concerns that starter Geno Smith is currently facing , and you could argue it would be much more valuable to keep those picks instead of giving up one to land O'Connell.
Sure, this is a team that has dealt with its fair share of injuries throughout the season and has struggled to remain at full strength, but that is still no excuse for the lack of adjustments and conservative approach that continue to plague Glenn on the sidelines, with New York's season continuing to unravel.
You cannot argue with the talent spread throughout the Jets' depth chart, but this is still a roster that is far from complete and one that can certainly benefit from a trio of first-round picks if used correctly on the right players.
For starters, the defense has been a mess all season, particularly its third-worst run defense (135.3 ypg) and repeated struggles from the linebackers . Additionally, the offense has struggled to convert third downs and ranks last in red-zone efficiency (37.9%), some obvious signs that change should be on the way at some point in the immediate future.
With an NFC North title in 2022 and a much better overall record, there is no doubt that O'Connell would be an upgrade over Glenn. At the same time, is he really worth the Jets giving up a first-round pick for?
With an unproven track record in the playoffs and, most recently, a disappointing 2025 season that culminated in the Vikings missing the playoffs altogether with a 9-8 record, that is certainly debatable.
Until the Vikings reunited with QB Kirk Cousins at the trade deadline and came away with a 30-10 win over the Packers last Sunday—only their second game with at least 30 points this season—the Vikings struggled at QB and had to rely on their top-ranked defense (14 ppg) to do the heavy lifting. O'Connell put his faith in Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz, only for neither to be the answer.
There was also the J.J. McCarthy saga: the 2024 first-rounder battled numerous injuries and accounted for more interceptions (12) than passing TDs (11) during his second season before getting traded to the Giants.
Considering the conundrum the Jets currently face at QB with the uncertainty facing Smith and the timidness that rookie Cade Klubnik showed in his first regular-season appearance against the Bills, it is fair to question if they want a similar situation to the one that transpired with McCarthy and the Vikings when searching for their franchise QB.
At this point, there is still plenty of time for Klubnik to continue to develop and for Smith to potentially lead this team to some wins if he can stay healthy, but it is also time to start looking ahead and get a feel for what the future might hold in Gotham.
With multiple coaches finding themselves in hot water to begin Week 11 and questions surrounding overall execution on the field, there will definitely be changes in store.
The upside is there with O'Connell, especially compared to Glenn's disastrous tenure with the Jets. However, the former's lack of postseason success and recent QB struggles make this a risky trade that may not be worth it for a Jets team that has a lot of draft capital.

title: 5 Things Darren Mougey Has Done Right to Fix Jets in 2026 and Beyond
full_text:
It's easy to look at the current record of the New York Jets and declare that head coach Aaron Glenn and general manager Darren Mougey are a package deal. After all, their 5-22 record together is among the worst in team history.
But context must be included when talking about the Jets' current structure. Glenn was hired before Mougey, and while the roster has improved greatly, the coaching has not . At this moment, it's easy to see a path to New York keeping Mougey past 2026 and moving on from Glenn entirely.
If that were to happen, New York needs to look only at five decisions from Mougey that have proven to be right for the franchise's future.
Sometimes an extension for a productive player on a bad roster isn't in the best interest of the organization. Mougey understands that well - it's one of the reasons why two of his replacements this year have been such massive upgrades.
Mougey upgraded at left guard and kicker this offseason. Offensively, the team let John Simpson walk in free agency, believing they could find someone cheaper and better than the veteran guard. Dylan Parham was signed to a two-year deal to be his replacement. All he has done is become the sixth-best guard in football. Simpson, meanwhile, has been average at best.
The same could be said at kicker. Nick Folk had an excellent season in 2025, but New York let him walk to Atlanta. After a position battle, the team found Jason Sanders, and the former All-Pro has gone 25-for-28 on field goals. Meanwhile, the Falcons released Folk.
Understanding when to let good players go is important for a quality general manager. Replacing those players with upgrades is even more important. And that's what Mougey has done this season alone.
Geno Smith is incredibly important to the Jets, not just for the 2026 season, but beyond that as well. New York needs a veteran quarterback they can rely on not only to bridge the gap to a future rookie, but also to be someone capable of playing good football and leading by example.
The best plan for the Jets is to draft a quarterback and have him set behind Smith for the 2027 season. This is the same plan the Kansas City Chiefs ran with Patrick Mahomes when he was made a first-round pick in 2017. Other examples like Tom Brady, Carson Palmer, Drew Brees, Phillip Rivers,  and Eli Manning also fit the idea of the Jets pairing Smith with a rookie signal-caller.
Until the Jets draft a quarterback who can win them games, the team will continue to struggle. The good news is that their current plan for the room is the one that has been tried and tested to be successful. And Mougey should be commended for it.
How he takes the rookie quarterback, and if that player develops, will be the next stage of that process.
The worst mistake New York could have made this season would have been going overboard to surround the current coaching staff with weapons. Trading 2027 or 2028 draft capital at the deadline to bolster the current team would not have changed their outlook this season. It wouldn't have saved Glenn, nor would it have altered the team's current 2-8 record.
Mougey has done a good job of understanding where the roster is. Last season, they were bad enough that acquiring draft capital for the likes of Quinnen Williams and Sauce Gardner would help the team's future.
This year, the team improved its talent and understood that the best way to build toward 2026 was to add it with draft picks, not with deadline acquisitions. Unlike the team's head coach, the Jets have a general manager with a modern plan who gets what needs to happen to get there.
It's important for teams to find value across the roster. One thing that the Jets have actually done well is finding players that many wouldn't expect to fill needs, and doing so at a very reasonable price.
This season has been a good example of that. New York signed edge rusher Kingsley Enagbare to a one-year deal worth just $10 million. Safety Dane Belton signed another one-year deal worth $4 million. Other free-agent pickups like Dylan Parham have also been a quality value.
However, Mougey's free agent history isn't a perfect run . Misses on Demario Davis, Justin Fields, and Joseph Ossai haven't helped the team as much as many would have hoped. That said, New York's goal is to improve the current roster. Unequivocally, the Jets have done it, and it is due to Mougey understanding areas of need and market value for each.
No general manager is above mistakes. Even the elites make them over the course of their career.
Great general managers, though, don't let their mistakes become long-term issues. The San Francisco 49ers whiffed on Trey Lance in 2021, but responded by drafting Brock Purdy. That first-round mistake, therefore, isn't as bad as it could have been.
The good thing Mougey has done is not make long-term mistakes. Many of the draft picks that have yet to pan out for the team are late-round selections. No GM is going to get fired over that. Even free agent signings that have failed do not put the Jets in a hole in terms of dead cap or future spending.
Mougey hasn't been perfect with the Jets. But he hasn't made the crippling mistakes that other executives have made with the team. For Joe Douglas, it was selecting Zach Wilson, trading for Haason Reddick, and whiffing on the offensive line.
Mougey hasn't gotten to that point yet. And therefore should get more chances moving forward.

title: Jets Shed Light on Their D'Angelo Ponds Feelings After Quiet Week 10
full_text:
Do the New York Jets have a plan for slot cornerback D'Angelo Ponds? The second-round pick received his second start of the season last week against Buffalo, but only played seven snaps.
Part of that decision came down to their opponent. Buffalo ran wild on New York to the tune of over 200 yards in a 31-12 blowout. Because of Buffalo's rushing success, the Jets opted to play former mid-round pick Malachi Moore four times as many snaps as Ponds.
That doesn't mean the the rookie played poorly, though.
Speaking to reporters in his new role as defensive play-caller, coordinator Brian Duker gave the Indiana prospect a major vote of confidence going into their next showdown against the Los Angeles Chargers.
Duker was clear. Despite playing only seven snaps in the team's loss, Ponds put forth the kind of game that the team was looking for over the last few weeks.
"I thought he did a nice job, probably his best game yet this past weekend," Duker said. "I thought his execution was the cleanest, that's probably the best way to say it. His executions of his assignment, where he was supposed to be, leverages, all those types of things."
So if the team believed that Ponds played well on Sunday, then why exactly did they play him significantly less than Moore?
The answer to that is New York's failing on defense. The Jets' front seven has been gutted consistently due to injuries and their focus on playing four downlinemen has put them in situations they can't stop at this point. By adding a bigger player in Moore, the team hopes a third safety will be better than adding a third cornerback on the field.
It's a sign that the team still needs to see more from Ponds in run defense as well.
With the Jets sitting at 2-8, there should be little the team needs to see more of from the safety room. It would be best for the team to play Ponds as much as possible to determine what kind of player he can be. Can he handle being a boundary corner despite his size? Is he just a slot player?
These are questions that can't be answered yet. By season's end, they must have one. New York has done a poor job of putting young players in the best positions possible. Ponds has been a good example of this. He hasn't been given enough of an opportunity to really know what kind of performer he can be.
But if they are to improve beyond 2027, the team will need to actually play them. If Ponds had the "best game" of his young career, then he will need more playing time altogether.

title: 3 Jets Would Be the Winners of a Potential Kevin O’Connell Trade
full_text:
The New York Jets have reached the point in the season where fans and media are speculating about a new head coach. New York holds a 2-8 record through 10 weeks, and every loss seems to be another nail in Aaron Glenn’s head-coaching coffin .
ESPN's Rich Cimini threw out Minnesota Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell as a surprise candidate on the Jets Collective podcast (h/t UStadium) as speculation continues over who will be the Jets' next head coach.
New York would have to make a trade for the Vikings' head coach, with O’Connell still under contract in Minnesota, but the coach would immediately impact the team. The fifth-year head coach has a 50-27 record and has fielded at least a seven-win team every year during his tenure. If New York traded for the head coach, these three Jets would immediately benefit from Kevin O’Connell’s arrival.
Wilson would arguably benefit most from the Jets trading for the Vikings’ head coach. O’Connell has experience with a top-five receiver in Justin Jefferson. That experience would do wonders in unlocking the 26-year-old. Wilson has shown he has the talent to be a top receiver in the NFL; O’Connell could be the one to elevate the Jet to that level.
Justin Jefferson has averaged 9.24 targets per game during O’Connell’s tenure in Minnesota. Over that time frame, Wilson averaged 8.92 targets. The Minnesota coach clearly sees the value in getting a number-one receiver touches throughout the season. If New York were to trade for O’Connell, Wilson could immediately slot into the Justin Jefferson role in the Jets’ offense.
Wilson’s lack of usage in 2026 has been a glaring issue for a middling Jets offense. O'Connell acquisition seems likely to fix that. Wilson would be a day-one beneficiary if this speculation becomes reality.
Rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq would also improve with the arrival of the 41-year-old. Sadiq was drafted with high expectations and has already shown the type of game-breaking talent he possesses. The rookie has put up a 22-238-1 stat line this season, but O’Connell could take him to the next level.
The Vikings traded for T.J. Hockenson in O’Connell’s first season with the team. Since then, Hockenson has not had fewer than 50 receptions in seasons in which he has played at least 11 games. Sadiq is arguably more talented than Hockenson. With O’Connell at the helm, Jets fans would have hope that Sadiq could have seasons like Hockenson’s 2023, when he posted a 95-960-5 stat line.
Max Brosmer, Joshua Dobbs, Sam Darnold, J.J. McCarthy — these are just half the quarterbacks O’Connell has coached to a win. The coach has an offense that Kirk Cousins walked back into after three seasons away from Minnesota and threw two touchdowns to beat the Packers in Week 10. One would think that offense would follow O’Connell to New York.
Regardless of who is throwing passes for New York next season, fans would love to see O’Connell as a coach. The head coach has shown he can win and that his offense works. Even McCarthy, who many see as the coach’s biggest mistake, won his last four starts as a Viking. Whether it is Geno Smith, Cade Klubnik, a rookie, or any other option, their skills would be enhanced by O’Connell.

title: Geno Smith’s Injury Creates Unique Conundrum About Jets’ Future
full_text:
It is Aaron Glenn's best interest to win as many games as possible down the stretch to try and prove to New York Jets ownership he's still the right man for the job.
At 2-8, though, what is in Glenn's best interest may not be the same for the Jets' franchise.
New York has been outcoached and outplayed for a majority of their games. As things stand, their current record seats them with the fourth overall pick in the 2027 draft. That pick could get worse, or improve, depending on how the Jets play down the stretch.
What Jets fans are frustrated most by, though, is their belief that the team is talented enough to win some games in their final seven contests and knock themselves out of a top pick, and a rookie quarterback. That belief changes with starting quarterback Geno Smith's injury, though. And if the quarterback isn't healthy enough to play on Sunday, New York's draft plans might be getting a whole lot better.
Glenn announced Wednesday that the ankle injury Smith suffered in last week's game against Buffalo would leave him limited in practice. How he responds to the injury could very well determine whether he plays against the Los Angeles Chargers or not.
"We'll see how the week goes," Glenn said when asked if Smith will be playing.
New York could very well be using gamesmanship by not announcing its starting QB plans. As things stand, Jets on SI have been told to expect Smith to push to play without any issues against the Chargers.
But is that best for what New York needs?
Smith has been a very competent quarterback this season. His 12 touchdowns and three interceptions are among the best touchdown-to-interception ratios the team has seen from a quarterback in years.
Could he lead the team to a victory over Los Angeles? Absolutely, especially with the Chargers at 1-8.
"That's the plan," Smith said after practice on Wednesday about whether he will play Sunday. "You obviously have to take it day-by-day, but that's the plan."
But the Smith decision is the perfect example of a team's goal being different from the staff's or locker room's. New York's players want to finally see wins on their schedule. They want to know their talents aren't being wasted.
The front office, though, has to take things where they are and understand the long-term benefits of losing out, or at least enough to secure a top pick.
That's why Smith would play beyond anything else on Sunday, even if it means potentially winning a game and hurting the team's chances at a top pick in April.
And why is absence could help the team far beyond this season.

title: 3 Jets Coaches Whose Jobs Should Be in Jeopardy to Begin Week 11
full_text:
Coming off their latest humiliating divisional loss after last Sunday's 31-12 defeat to the Bills, the Jets head into a two-game road trip that begins with a Week 11 meeting against the Chargers with their focus on ending a five-game losing streak.
With a 2-8 record through 10 games, there are clearly some glaring issues that continue to persist and there are only so many roster moves a front office can make throughout the season. Aside from trading former safety Andre Cisco to the Lions ahead of the trade deadline, this is still the same roster that began the season.
With two favorable matchups against the Chargers and Dolphins coming up before the Week 13 bye, it would not be unexpected to see some shifting responsibilities on the coaching staff or even some firings. After all, head coach Aaron Glenn just gave up his play-calling duties to defensive coordinator Brian Duker, although it remains to be seen who has the role going forward.
As they prepare for a trip out west to face the 1-8 Chargers, here's a look at three Jets coaches whose jobs should be in jeopardy going into Week 11.
With a 5-22 record as the HC of the Jets and an 0-9 mark against divisional competition, Glenn is simply on borrowed time at this point and could easily be the first coach out the door if Gang Green's struggles carry over into a pair of games they should have a shot to win.
While the Jets have been competitive and should have a much better record than they currently do with some better decision-making, that is ultimately not the case due to Glenn's repeated inability to make second-half adjustments and his conservative approach in goal-to-go and short-yardage situations.
Not only did Glenn hand his defensive play-calling over to Duker in the Week 10 loss to the Bills, which was a bad look by itself considering he has referred to play-calling as his "superpower," but his decision to settle for field goals when the Bills were punching it in for touchdowns remains a concern going forward.
"It's hard to win games when you operate that way," Glenn said, per Jets on SI's Nick Faria . "I think one thing we do a good job of is actually moving the ball, but once we get there that's what we've got to get better at and those are things we've got to continue to work on."
Sure, it was another injury-riddled loss to the Bills as the depth of this Jets roster continues to get tested. That said, the results have just not been there on the field, healthy or not, during Glenn's Jets tenure so far. Unless he can make the appropriate adjustments and win the next two games like he should be expected to, it will just be a matter of whether the front office gives him the ax immediately or waits for the season to end.
While some may argue that Reich could move into the role of interim HC if the Jets elect to fire Glenn during the season, especially due to his previous coaching experience with the Panthers and Colts, he is in just as much hot water as Glenn due to his failure to consistently get the ball to his best players.
To his credit, WR1 Garrett Wilson led the team in receptions (seven), targets (14) and receiving yards (106) in the loss to the Bills, but that has not always been the case throughout the season. On top of that, Reich's play-calling in short-yardage situations, third down and in the red zone has been questionable to say the least.
Those struggles and repeated decisions to settle for field goals eventually caught up to the Jets when Bills quarterback Josh Allen found wide receiver DJ Moore for a 45-yard TD (h/t NFL) to extend Buffalo's lead to 12 and take control late in the third quarter.
ALLEN TO DJ MOORE FOR 6 BUFvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/hfrUwKQlws
Reich has some opportunities in front of him to make his seat a little cooler, but if he cannot consistently find a way to get his best players the ball and end Gang Green's current nine-quarter drought without a TD, he could be in trouble.
Although Duker did not have any prior experience calling plays when Glenn handed the duties over to him in Week 10, he is no stranger to the Jets HC, most recently serving as defensive assistant, safeties coach and defensive backs coach while Glenn was the DC with the Lions.
Still, it was an ugly debut for Duker as the Jets were outscored, 21-6, in the second half and allowed the Bills rushing attack to combine for 201 yards. The Jets have now allowed their last three opponents to eclipse 30 points and have the third-worst rushing defense (135.3 YPG), so it is not like this was a favorable spot for Duker to be put in.
Despite that, the Jets currently have three first-round draft picks and the pressure continues to mount regarding who is going to be part of this staff for the next phase of the rebuild. It was just one game for Duker, but Glenn's hesitancy to commit to him as the defensive play-caller shows there are still some concerns there, especially if no gains are made against two of the league's three worst scoring offenses.

title: 3 Pending Jets Free Agents That Deserve New Contracts Despite Disastrous Season
full_text:
Why would a 2-8 team in the NFL be willing to retain starters on their struggling lineup?
What if I told you there were players on the New York Jets deserving of new contracts, even if they haven't fixed much of what has plagued the roster this year?
New York has several pending free agents going into the 2027 offseason. Many have performed poorly this year due to a number of different factors . However, there are those who have played well enough to get more time in Florham Park.
Today, we'll go through the three most important players New York needs to re-sign here.
If New York let all their pending defensive free agents walk, most fans would understand. The one player who deserves a new contract, though, is safety Dane Belton.
The former New York Giant has become an everydown player for New York, with the third-best run defense grade of any safety in the league and an average mark in coverage. Those numbers alone are good enough to keep him on the team over the next few years.
In-the-box safeties rarely get massive payouts, but the Jets need a starter opposite Minkah Fitzpatrick next season, and Belton is the obvious choice to fill that role.
It's become almost a foregone conclusion that the Jets will take a quarterback in the 2027 draft. How they surround that rookie quarterback will remain a big question mark, though.
The most consistent and efficient way to allow a young signal-caller to develop is by putting him behind a veteran leader and an offensive minded coaching staff that will keep one system in place. Whether the Jets draft CJ Carr, Drew Mestemaker, or Darian Mensah, the team should follow that system to build around them.
That means keeping Geno Smith at all costs.
Smith has thrown 12 touchdowns to just three interceptions this season. He hasn't been a world-beater, but he's been competent at a time when so few things are working for New York.
New York should extend Smith into 2027 on a starting salary to allow them the chance to grow an incoming rookie behind a proven veteran. The process has worked for many teams before. It's time for the Jets to join in that plan.
Depth is incredibly important in the NFL, especially on the offensive line. New York hasn't gotten the best from Jordan Meredith this season, but if the team were smart, they should sign him to a limited extension thanks to his versatility and starting experience.
New York has a lot of issues to fix this offseason. One group that doesn't need to be overhauled, though, is the offensive line. With Parham returning, the team really only needs an upgrade at center to round out the group.
And with Meredith having experience at both guard and center, the team should be in a good position to bring him back and not worry too much about the group's depth going forward.

title: 5 Biggest Mistakes Made by Aaron Glenn Since Becoming Jets Head Coach
full_text:
By the time the Aaron Glenn era ends by the end of the season (as many expect), the New York Jets will have gone through a two-year run of futility rarely seen across NFL season.
Going into Week 11, the Jets are 5-22 under Glenn as head coach and 0-9 in the AFC East . The numbers are second-worst in team history, behind only Rich Kotite in the 1990s. There are a number of reasons why the team has struggled during this stretch.
But five mistakes matter most when we look back at the Glenn era.
There will be people tired of the idea the Jets should have kept Rodgers instead of moving on as they did following a five-win season in 2024.
But it's hard to ignore what could have been had Glenn and the Jets been more willing to keep the future Hall-of-Famer around, especially in an offense like the one they currently have.
Rodgers led the Pittsburgh Steelers to the AFC North title in 2025. They are well on their way to another playoff appearance this season as well. Part of that is due to their defense and run game, but Rodgers deserves credit as well.
Had Glenn looked to establish himself more, and given more of a buffer for his coaching abilities, keeping Rodgers would have made things easier from a winning perspective. Maybe the team would have still lost a lot of games, but fans would have targeted Rodgers more than Glenn after his first season.
Instead, Glenn's decisions were put in the spotlight from the very beginning. Moving on from Rodgers made the team worse last season. And it hasn't helped their chances in 2026 either.
At some point, the Jets and their fans are going to realize: introductory press conferences are the most meaningless things for head coaches. Guys who struggle and get made fun of for poor quotes at the beginning can turn into excellent coaches. People who give stellar answers may not know what to do once the headsets come on.
From the very beginning of his hiring, Glenn has focused heavily on keeping his passion and swagger on point. That has included answers and a showmanship bravado that can endear itself to fans...when a team is winning.
The problems come becuase Glenn's passionate quotes have rarely been met with on-field success. Whether it was commenting on a player's lack of breakout status due to "coaching" or that the team wanted to build something "fans could be proud of" or any other passionate stance Glenn has held.
There are several quotes Glenn has made over the last two years that have backfired spectacularly. With each whiff, his mistakes at the podium just compound his biggest issues.
Every coach wants their teams to look and play a certain way. But there's a difference between wanting a team to be tough and physical, and forcing a roster to play a specific strategic gameplan regardless of their opponent.
New York wants their corners to be excellent in man coverage. They want their defense to play a base 3-4 scheme. Nevermind the fact they don't have the players for each scheme, they simply want to play that way regardless of outcome.
Offensively, it's even worse. New York has all the talent in the world to be a pass first unit and force defenses to react to their talent and scheme. But the Jets are more focused on reacting to what the defense is doing, instead of dictating play. They push to be a run-first team, even when the roster is best used as a spread-out run-and-gun unit.
Good coaches alter their stragetic plans for the team they have. Not the team they want.
Glenn's big mistake is his inability to adjust to anything the NFL is putting out, instead expecting his style to win football games.
This was one that many people thought wouldn't be an issue going into Glenn's second season. With his decision to call plays defensively, he needed an experienced offensive mind to run the offense without needing his help.
But was Frank Reich the right choice? Hindsight is always 20/20, but not retaining young offensive coordinator Tanner Engstrand was clearly a mistake. Reich's offense this season has been stagnant despite better quarterback play, and better weapons across the board.
Engstrand's unit, while poor at times, had a scheme that used players all over the field, attacked matchups, and ultimately, was more effective despite the clear limitations brought to him at quarterback.
A big question should be what Engstrand could have done with Geno Smith as a starter this season, and with a full collection of weapons that the Jets have.
Instead, New York is seriously devoid of creativity this season and Reich is at the forefront of that issue. Because he wanted to replace Engstrand without realizing the benefits to keeping him, this mistake makes the list.
This is easily the most egregious of Glenn's mistakes. It's one to thing to whiff on a coaching hire, or at quarterback. These things can happen to an elite coach, let alone a bad one.
But Glenn's inability to understand analytics, and the importance of being aggressive at all times is his biggest weakness. It's a big reason why the team is 2-8 this season, and well on their way to another bottom-five finish around the NFL.
Glenn doesn't understand when to be aggressive. He'll be happy kicking field goals over going for it on fourth down to score touchdowns. He'll put in short yardage situations when the offense is moving. He sees a defense in the Jets that isn't the catalyst for the team, but wants to be the reason they win games.
Glenn's selective aggressiveness holds the Jets back. Sure, the roster may not be ready to beat the likes of Buffalo or Kansas City, but it's obvious around the league that teams know the coach won't make the right calls in order to help his team win in New York.
At this rate, with two years of tape, and two years of chances to fix it, Glenn's choice to be passive at all key moments will eventually be his undoing.

title: 3 WR Targets the Jets Need to Have on Their Radar After Omar Cooper Jr.‘s Injury
full_text:
With Garrett Wilson returning from the concussion protocol, the Jets entered their Week 10 matchup against the Bills with their original offensive starters for the first time since Week 1. However, the unit lasted just one play together, as rookie receiver Omar Cooper Jr. sustained an ankle injury.
This is the third time Cooper has had his right ankle rolled up this season, as Kenyon Sadiq was tackled into the back of his leg. The first incident happened in Week 1, which resulted in him landing on the injured reserve list, and the second occurred in Week 9.
Cooper underwent imaging on his ankle, and although the injury’s severity remains unclear, head coach Aaron Glenn told reporters Wednesday that he wouldn’t practice, per ESPN's Rich Cimini . While it’s still too early to rule him out for Sunday’s matchup against the Chargers, New York must have a backup plan ready in case he’s a no-go, especially with Isaiah Williams sidelined for Wednesday’s practice with a rib injury.
Other Jets injuries: Omar Cooper Jr (ankle) and Isaiah Williams (ribs) won't practice today. Joseph Ossai, Dylan Parham and Trevin Wallace will be limited. #Jets are opening the practice window for DT David Onyemata, who has been on IR for eight weeks.
With Glenn needing wins to have any chance of saving his job , the Jets must target veteran receivers in free agency or from other teams’ practice squads who can help contribute right away. With that in mind, here are three receivers New York must have on its radar.
Of the three receivers, Tyler Johnson is the only one who has ties to the Jets. He spent last season on New York’s practice squad, finishing the year with 12 receptions for 197 yards and a touchdown across 11 games.
Johnson briefly returned to the practice squad this fall after Cooper was placed on injured reserve, but he was released without appearing in a game. Given his experience and familiarity with the offense, the Jets could bring Johnson back and have him suit up for the team’s game against the Chargers.
While he isn’t as impactful as Cooper, Johnson is someone New York can trust immediately. He knows the system and has experience playing in the slot, lining up there for 41.4% of his career snaps, per Pro Football Focus.
Although he’s not an explosive downfield receiver, the Jets could use him in the short-to-intermediate areas on slants and crossers to pick up some yards.
K.J. Osborn doesn’t have the experience or familiarity with the Jets like Johnson; however, he’s arguably the better choice. The former 2020 fifth-round selection was a solid complementary option during his three years with the Vikings, registering 160 receptions for 1,865 yards and three touchdowns.
Regarded for his versatility, Osborn was effective both inside in the slot and on the outside. Although he doesn’t have elite top-end speed, he excelled as a vertical threat in Minnesota. The Vikings prioritized pushing the ball downfield.
In a limited role, Osborn can provide a similar spark. Despite not being as aggressive this season, Geno Smith likes to take shots downfield, and the Jets already have several vertical weapons.
Osborn's downside, however, is that he hasn’t had success outside Minnesota. He’s spent the past three seasons with four different teams and hasn’t appeared in a single offensive snap since the 2024 season.
But if Cooper is sidelined, Osborn should be on New York’s radar.
Samuel is the most productive player of the three and, at his peak, is the best. The former Ohio State Buckeye is a complete offensive weapon and has been used as such over his nine-year career, lining up in the slot and at running back.
While the Jets don’t need him in the backfield, they could use his explosiveness on the inside if Cooper misses time. Samuel has proven to be a quality playmaker in his career, with 1,509 of his 3,799 receiving yards coming after the catch.
Even though injuries and regression have slowed him down, he’s still a reliable pass-catcher who can gain extra yardage with his speed. New York can rely on him in a limited role and use him as a gadget player to ease pressure on Wilson and Adonai Mitchell to consistently create separation.
